item.title: Fantasy Football: DeVonta Smith's target share with Tanner McKee at QB, plus more key stats that may go overlooked from Week 6
item.description: Joel Smyth covers important stats from Week 6 that may go overlooked for fantasy football.
item.content:encoded:
In fantasy football, you have to look back to move forward. Fantasy points are the goal, but how a player gets there is the key. Analyst Joel Smyth breaks down 8 numbers to know from Week 6 in order to win your matchup in Week 7 and beyond.

29

Targets in Germie Bernard’s three games playing with the starting unit. Eight targets in Week 2 without Michael Pittman Jr., up to nine last week with three wide receiver injuries and 12 on Sunday as the team’s WR2 (only 27% of routes run in the other three games). With so many injuries in Pittsburgh, the rookie stepped up, running 78% of routes and bringing in 11 receptions. Aaron Rodgers, who’s known for a lack of trust with young receivers, has been loving Bernard so far, praising him off the field and targeting him on the field. As the short-area slot receiver, Bernard’s average depth of target was an extremely low 1.83 yards. He meshes with Rodgers' veteran play style and has an increased floor in PPR leagues. I would expect this role to stick once the other Steelers receivers return. ​

3

Red-zone targets for Colston Loveland upon Caleb Williams' return. A great fantasy day that could have gone way better (to be pessimistic) if he was able to get into the end zone on his opportunities deep in the red area. Entering the day, Loveland had an oddly high 2.7 “expected touchdowns” based on his volume, where and how much. As you probably know, he scored zero until this Sunday.

Yet, once again he was out at the one yard line on one catch, and failed to settle down on another route to convert an easy end-zone target. The volume is there, the skillset is there and the touchdowns should keep coming in this offense. The Bears’ offense leads the NFL with 101 plays in the red zone and I believe Loveland will have more than one touchdown over the next 101.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

18

Routes run for Luther Burden III in Week 6. Rome Odunze finished at 40, Loveland at 33, Kalif Raymond right above at 25 and even Cole Kmet at 23. Burden and Raymond have been fluctuating throughout the year as the third receiver on a team that plays a lot of two-tight end sets. Burden managed to finish with eight receptions on eight targets, but the long-term consistency is not as secure. Williams isn’t always going to go 30 for 36 and Burden’s lack of red-zone snaps and routes in general may keep him as a more volatile fantasy player. Although Chicago played 18 red-zone snaps as mentioned above, Burden was only out on the field for three of those plays, running one route. It’s a glass-half-full or glass-half-empty situation: he’s managed to produce (for the most part) in a limited role so far; it may limit him going forward, and at the same time an increase can turn him into a fantasy star.

31.8%

Target share in DeVonta Smith’s first full game with Tanner McKee. Off the injury report, Smith was targeted 14 times by the Eagles’ backup quarterback. McKee previously only had 11 pass plays in his career with Smith on the field, targeting him on six of those plays for 86 receiving yards and a TD. They continued building on that small sample size against a Panthers defense that was without two of its top corners in the lineup.

The difference in efficiency from Jalen Hurts to McKee is slightly made up for in the passing volume. It was McKee’s third career start, and his third career game with over 40 passing attempts as this offense transforms without Hurts under center, and for this season, without a run game to lean on. McKee is looking like one of the more positive backup QB situations based on his target share, although he may be more matchup-dependent without Hurts under center.

0.89

Fantasy points per route for Puka Nacua when Davante Adams is off the field since 2025. For comparison, Nacua’s 0.78 pts/route led the NFL last season, in a year where his routes were limited due to Adams being the wide receiver in on three-TE sets. Basically, he’s going to go nuclear if Adams were to miss any time. Nacua’s connection with Matthew Stafford has been flawed at times this season, with his catchable target rate dropping from 85.9% to 76.9%, and yet, he’s still averaged 23.0 PPR PPG with only one receiving touchdown! He could very well join the tier of Jahmyr Gibbs and Bijan Robinson if Adams were to miss time.

11-14

The red-zone snaps for the Rams running backs the last two weeks, slightly favoring Kyren Williams over Blake Corum. Williams’ bellcow role we saw from the first month seemed to have decreased, but after going through the numbers, it was hard to see much of a difference. Corum’s snap share stayed the exact same and his rush share was up by just 1%. The red-zone work, however, flipped back to how the second half of 2025 played out. After Williams had 30 of 32 red-zone snaps, Corum has had nearly 50% the last two weeks, equaling two touchdowns. It doesn’t ruin Williams’ fantasy value, but he is sadly trending towards a lower-end RB1 profile rather than top-five after starting the first month as the fantasy RB5.

23%

Targets per route this season for Ja'Kobi Lane… Okay, if you count his nullified TD via penalty target. After being the Ravens’ training camp star, Lane looked like he was on his way to a big day in Week 1 before going down with an injury. Week 6 was his first day back from a wrist injury and he was immediately relied on after WR Rashod Bateman aggravated a shoulder injury Sunday.

Three of those targets (really four) were red-zone targets, making Lane’s usage that much more interesting. In games with Lamar Jackson, the Ravens’ offense ranks inside the top-10 with nearly four red-zone drives per game, and unlike past seasons, doesn’t have a large share of the production going to the tight end position. Zay Flowers will get a lot of the designed and underneath work, but Lane can be the top contested-catch option in the red zone going forward. ​

82%

Route share in Omar Cooper Jr.’s return. Safe to say he’s passed Isaiah Williams (6% routes). The rookie first-rounder entered the day with one route on the season and then barely came off the field in Week 6. He had multiple screens, led the team in targets and played 68% of passing plays as the Jets’ slot receiver. He didn’t let it go to waste either, bringing in a 48-yard TD as well as a near second score that was called back by penalty. Cooper is an easy add on waivers this week, but also is another threat to Garrett Wilson’s volume along with an injured Adonai Mitchell as well as Kenyon Sadiq, who was limited on Sunday. With New York still being a shaky offense as a whole, Wilson’s high-end fantasy value is more reliant on his volume.

item.title: After Chris Ballard's firing, Colts find themselves staring at a major overhaul
item.description: The Colts could be facing major changes
item.content:encoded:
Even if you question what good firing a general manager during the season does, it wasn't a major surprise when the Indianapolis Colts fired GM Chris Ballard on Monday.

The Colts have made the playoffs once since 2018 and have no playoff wins since then. Their best record since 2021 is 9-8, and they've gone 8-9 in each of the two seasons. This season they sit at 2-4, with a loss to the previously winless Titans on Sunday and victories over one- and two-win teams.

Ballard's biggest problem was getting the quarterback spot right. When he arrived, Andrew Luck was in place, and his sudden retirement set the franchise back. But Ballard has had the better part of a decade to get this position right, and it just hasn't happened.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

The Colts might have thought they had their guy in Daniel Jones a year ago when the Colts hit 8-2 and appeared to be a playoff squad. That's when they traded for cornerback Sauce Gardner — a move that blew up in their faces.

Now the question is what happens next.

Carlie Irsay-Gordon has been taking a hands-on approach to ownership of the club since her father's passing, even donning headsets during games to get a better feel how the organization runs, top to bottom. It would be hard to imagine that more significant changes will follow eventually.

"​Making this change during the season was a deliberate decision," Irsay-Gordon said in her statement. "Waiting would only delay the important work that needs to begin now. We will conduct a thorough search for our next general manager and take the time necessary to identify the right leader for the future of this organization."

Does this mean changes to the coaching staff will follow? A trade-deadline purge? A new quarterback next offseason? Let's break down what's next for the Colts during this transition period.

Trade deadline looms, and the Colts should be sellers

Let's first be transparent: Irsay-Gordon also said the Colts plan to be competitive.

"I also want to be clear: this decision does not change our goals for the season. We have a lot of football in front of us, and I expect us to compete, improve, and win football games," Irsay-Gordon's statement also said. 

That's a noble intention, but there's also a cold reality. They're 2-4 and likely need to look vastly better over the next few weeks to avoid the inevitable. 

The big picture is that the Gardner trade, which sapped the Colts of their 2026 and 2027 first-round picks, has significantly damaged their offseason draft-pick lot. What stings a little extra is that the 2027 NFL Draft appears to be one of the more top-heavy classes in the past few years, and the Colts would be picking sixth overall if the season ended today. Instead, the Jets will enjoy that windfall, wherever the pick ends up.

The Colts have to consider moving on from some of their more valuable pieces as a way of helping recoup some of the lost value. Irsay-Gordon expressed a desire to expeditiously move on from Ballard, and she should endorse similar aggression when it comes to moving assets, starting with prior to the trade deadline in the coming weeks.

One obvious one would be defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, who is 32 years old and headed for free agency in the spring. There likely would be multiple teams interested in his services. Grover Stewart is 33 and in the same position. Either or both could be available.

Other pieces to consider moving: wide receiver Josh Downs and safety Cam Bynum. Both are younger pieces who could fetch decent value if moved. 

But what about Jonathan Taylor? From a value perspective, it would make sense to unload a pricy running back with an injury history and arguably at his peak (or moving past it) with nearly 2,000 career touches. 

There also could be a conversation about moving offensive guard Quenton Nelson, who is also in a free-agent season. The question is whether Irsay-Gordon has the same sentimentality as her father, Jim Irsay, who was known to be fond of both Taylor and Nelson and likely viewed them as career-long Colts.

In-season general manager firings tend to be more rare, but when they happen, it can be an indication of a fire sale to come. This played out in Miami after GM Chris Grier was fired during the regular season a year ago. Jaelen Phillips was dealt, and the Dolphins dangled Jaylen Waddle and Bradley Chubb, eventually trading Waddle in the offseason.

Barring a quick Colts turnaround, it would be hard to imagine they're not open for business, and they have plenty of options to move.

Quarterback future looking dim, with limited options

The Colts' move to re-sign Jones last offseason isn't standing the test of time. Jones was off to a career-best flourish to start last season, but he hit a wall when injuries mounted, eventually missing the rest of the season with a ruptured Achilles tendon.

Jones' quick return from the injury suffered in December should be viewed as a strong commitment to his rehab and professionalism, but the product he's put out there this season hasn't been a match in excellence. Jones ranks near the bottom of the rankings among most qualified passers. He's had interceptions in every game but one (and two in the loss to the Titans on Sunday) and is on pace for his worst career completion percentage (59.6).

Remember, too, that the Colts allowed Michael Pittman Jr. to walk, knowing they couldn't keep him, Jones and Alec Pierce. Right now, Pierce is on IR, with five catches in two games so far this season.

One way or another, the Colts are more likely to move on from Jones this offseason. Sure, he still has time to turn things around, but counting on that feels awfully risky. 

We know Anthony Richardson's story, and he doesn't realistically figure to be among the potential solutions, either. Richardson had his chances to claim the Colts' starting job, and his failures were a big strike against Ballard.

The next general manager is going to have to figure out how best to acquire a quarterback this offseason and make it work without a first-round pick.

Even if there are reasonably interesting QB prospects who linger long enough to be available in Round 2 of the draft, the most prudent and likely option would be a veteran who outplayed his welcome elsewhere, perhaps similar to Kyler Murray, Kirk Cousins or Tua Tagovailoa — a bridge option until they find better.

There will be options, but the quality of those options will be far below "unquestioned franchise starter." This is just another indication of the breadth of the Colts' rebuild, especially if they sell off pieces at the deadline.

item.title: NFL Monday Night Football preview: 49ers try to stay undefeated vs. Commanders
item.description: The Commanders are looking for a win to get back in the NFC East race.
item.content:encoded:
As we found out in Week 6, and see pretty much every week in the NFL, being expected to win doesn't mean too much.

Teams like the Los Angeles Rams and Indianapolis Colts lost as significant favorites on Sunday, and perhaps that's a warning for the San Francisco 49ers.

The 49ers are 5-0. They and the Kansas City Chiefs are the only undefeated teams in the NFL. The 49ers face a Washington Commanders team that's 1-3-1 and coming off an embarrassing time-management debacle that cost them a chance to beat the New York Giants in overtime.

And that's the type of mismatch that we often see lead to a surprise outcome.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

The Commanders can be dangerous. They have a win over the Seahawks already. Jayden Daniels is back and healthy, and showed his playmaking skills with two long rushing touchdowns last week. Just because the Commanders have just one win doesn't mean they're not capable.

The 49ers are tough to beat, however. Brock Purdy has 13 passing touchdowns, which led the NFL after five weeks, and is in the early conversation for MVP. The offense as a whole has been fantastic early on, with new addition at receiver Mike Evans making a big impact already, and the defense has been a pleasant surprise. The defense ranked third in points allowed heading into this week. The 49ers have dealt with many injuries — they're especially thin at receiver with Deebo Samuel suffering a hamstring injury last week — but it hasn't stopped them.

The Commanders have a big challenge ahead to beat the 49ers on the road. But as we found out Sunday, it's a mistake to discount any team in the NFL.

Who needs it more?

The 49ers have already had a good Week 6. The Seahawks lost to the Broncos on Thursday night, then the Rams fell to 2-4 with a loss to the Cardinals. The 49ers would love to extend their lead in the NFC West but a loss wouldn't be too ruinous. The Commanders got off to a slow start this season and now need to steal a game or two in order to get back in the race in a soft NFC East. An upset win by the Commanders would put them only one game behind the Giants for first place. Washington needs it much more.

Key player: 49ers LB Fred Warner

The last off-ball linebacker to win NFL Defensive Player of the Year was Luke Kuechly in 2013. Before Kuechly, the last winner was Brian Urlacher in 2005. It won't be easy for Warner to win DPOY, but he'll have a case. Warner already has 50 tackles and leads the NFL with three forced fumbles. His Pro Football Focus grade is second among all inside linebackers (Jacksonville's Ventrell Miller is first). Warner's impact on the 49ers' defense is undeniable. San Francisco was fourth in defensive DVOA through five weeks and that is with Nick Bosa missing most of the season so far due to injury (Bosa will be out on Monday night as well). Warner will be instrumental in limiting the Commanders' offensive attack.

Betting market watch

The 49ers (-7.5) are healthy home favorites against the Commanders. Washington has spent all week dissecting and explaining what in the world went wrong at the end of a 27-27 tie against the New York Giants last week. After their Week 1 game in Australia, the 49ers haven't had to leave the West Coast (three straight home games and a trip to Seattle), so they'll certainly have the travel advantage. Mike Evans (questionable) is a big potential missing piece, but right now the 49ers (2-1 ATS at home) are playing too well and something tells me Washington hasn't healed from last week. The Commanders have allowed TDs on a league-worst 83.3% of red zone drives; the 49ers lead the NFL by scoring TDs on 87.5% of red zone drives. That's a bad combination for the Commanders' chances. — Ben Fawkes

Check out more of Ben's work at the Yahoo Sports betting hub.

Fantasy football storylines

It's fantasy's last call as the Niners and Commanders close out Week 6. Here are three themes to track from a fantasy perspective.

1. Can the Commanders cobble together a running game? With Jacory Croskey-Merritt unavailable, Washington will need to get creative — or perhaps junk the running game entirely. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler will get the first chances.

2. How do the 49ers work with or without Mike Evans? The estimable veteran didn't practice all week and really hasn't been 100 percent all year. It hasn't stopped him from being a fantasy star. We love QB Brock Purdy and play-calling genius Kyle Shanahan, but the Niners need to find solutions with a compromised Evans — or possibly without him.

3. How much will Jayden Daniels run? The third-year pro was not shy about scrambling last week, racking up 103 yards on the ground. He needs to be athletic and creative to play his best, but it also makes you worry, given his injury history. — Scott Pianowski

Check out more of Scott's work at the Yahoo Sports fantasy hub.

item.title: Seahawks signing veteran tight end Josiah Deguara to practice squad
item.description: The veteran’s addition comes after Elijah Arroyo's shoulder injury in Week 6.
item.content:encoded:
Ahead of a Week 7 clash against the still-undefeated Kansas City Chiefs, the Seattle Seahawks have added some depth to their tight end room.

Seventh-year pro Josiah Deguara was signed to the 17-man practice squad on Monday, ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler reported.

Deguara’s addition provides depth to a tight end corps that will potentially be thinner this week and beyond, after sophomore Elijah Arroyo suffered a shoulder injury during Thursday night’s loss to the Denver Broncos. While Arroyo’s status for Sunday is not yet clear, Deguara’s signing at least suggests it’s up in the air — if not trending downward. Seattle is slated for a Monday practice, and while no injury report is required, we should have an Arroyo update fairly soon.

Deguara, 29, was a third-round pick of the Green Bay Packers in 2020, and played four seasons with them catching 47 passes for 436 yards and two touchdowns. He spent 2024 with the Jaguars and 2025 with the Cardinals, catching three balls in both stops. The veteran bounced around during this year’s preseason, spending time with the Giants and 49ers before landing with the Eagles for a one-game stint. He was released by Philadelphia last week, after going back and forth between the team’s 53-man roster and practice squad.

Should Arroyo miss time with the shoulder injury suffered against the Broncos, Deguara could be elevated for Sunday Night Football against the Chiefs and make his Seahawks debut.

item.title: Report: Colts Assistant GM Ed Dodds will oversee personnel department in interim for 2026
item.description: The Colts reportedly made a move that was widely expected, as longtime assistant GM Ed Dodds will assume lead football operations in the interim for 2026.
item.content:encoded:
According to ESPN’s Stephen Holder, Indianapolis Colts assistant GM Ed Dodds will now assume overseeing the team’s personnel department as expected, in the aftermath of longtime GM Chris Ballard’s Monday firing:

That being said, Colts head coach Shane Steichen and his coaching staff will directly report to team ownership, meaning most likely, CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon in this instance.

Having served as Ballard’s ‘right hand man’ since 2018 as Colts assistant GM, Dodds has been consistently named a “hot name for future GM openings” on an annual basis.

He’s had a number of interviews with NFL teams with GM vacancies through past offseasons, even withdrawing from other teams’ interview processes because of the ownership fit and wanting to finish what he and Ballard initially started together in Indianapolis since 2017—where he began as the Colts senior personnel executive and scout from the Seattle Seahawks before being promoted by Ballard.

In the interim, despite his obvious loyalty and professional relationship with Ballard, this would seem like a great opportunity for him to get firsthand, hands on experience of what it’s like to be the top leader of a team’s football operations for the remainder of the 2026 campaign—even if he’s not the Colts GM going forward thereafter.

In my opinion, it would still make sense for the Colts to clean house entirely at year-end within their football operations department and get new leadership voices and a fresh perspective, which have been sorely needed.

item.title: Eagles News: “This offense is such a trainwreck”
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 10/19/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

Before we go blaming the offensive struggles on injuries alone, do recall that it wasn’t very good when they were healthier. And are this year’s injuries a good excuse for the offense looking bad last year as well? How about the offense looking confused from the first snap in the Eagles’ loss to the Carolina Panthers? Coaching is clearly part of the problem.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

Roob’s Observations as Eagles extend losing skid to four with loss to Panthers – NBCSP

This offense is such a trainwreck, and their issues go way behind missing Jalen Hurts. They scored two touchdowns Sunday against the Panthers and it seemed like a hell of a day. They’re averaging 14.6 points during the four-game losing streak. They’re averaging 219 yards per game during the losing streak. These numbers are just unfathomable. They haven’t had 300 yards in a game since Week 2. We could go on with first downs, passing yards, 3rd-down percentage, but you get the idea. They’re all just abysmal. Is it all Sean Mannion’s fault? Nah. But he certainly hasn’t distinguished himself in his first six games as Eagles offensive coordinator and play caller. Maybe things will get better when they get Landon Dickerson and Drew Kendall back and maybe Saquon will be back next week, although who really knows. This is all just such a mess right now. They got off to a decent start the first two weeks and has just spiraled downhill ever since. There’s so much to fix and I don’t even know how you go about starting. It just may be unfixable.

Let’s talk about which NFL coaches should be fired soon – SB Nation

Nick Sirianni — Philadelphia Eagles. There’s no sugarcoating what’s happened in Philly. This team is a mess. Injuries have wracked the team, seemingly finding a way to keep getting worse by the day. More and more players are hitting the injury report, entering IR, or just missing key snaps. Against the Panthers on Sunday the team did its best, but it was clear they just didn’t have enough players to really make an impact. At the center of everything is Nick Sirianni, who looks miserable trying to coach this season. Things weren’t great before the injuries, and now he’s forced to watch Tanner McKee, and a chorus of mediocre running backs try to form some semblance of an offense. The team is still decent defensively, but they’re banged up on that side too. It’s reached the point where it’s difficult to envision the Eagles winning many more games this year. That’s where the rub comes in, and what makes this so tricky. Sirianni does not to be fired based on the injuries and adversity he’s faced, especially when we look at his past history of success. The main issue is that if the Eagles end up with a very high draft pick, potentially in a spot to upgrade at quarterback — at what point is it worth trying to turn over a new leaf in the process? We have a scenario that feels somewhat similar to Doug Pederson. We had a Super Bowl-winning head coach who failed to follow up on the success, and owner Jeffrey Lurie believed that the long-term success of the franchise was more important than preserving the status quo, even if he thought Pederson was a decent coach. The team decided to part ways with their coach, Carson Wentz, draft a new QB, and install Nick Sirianni — ending a five-year tenure for all of them.

Jalen Hurts update: Eagles quarterback out for the season – BGN

It feels weird to pivot to the football ramifications of this news but it’s the reality the Eagles find themselves in as well. Tanner McKee is now the quarterback for the rest of the season. That is, unless they Eagles decide to eventually bench him for Cole Payton, Joe Milton III, or someone not currently on the roster. (We know it won’t be Andy Dalton, because he reportedly declined to re-sign with the Eagles and joined the Atlanta Falcons instead.)

Different QB, same problems: Is Sean Mannion’s system holding back the Eagles? – The Athletic

It would be a rationalization to blame injuries and exits. It happened too often with Hurts. It looked worse with McKee. And the constant is Mannion’s offense. “We have to do different things to get them going and score more points, plain and simple,” head coach Nick Sirianni said. “Everything’s on the table. To do the same thing over and over again and not get the results, that’d be foolish. Everything’s on the table of what we need to do to be able to put points on the board.” “Everything” being on the table is wide-ranging and ambiguous. It doesn’t endorse the status quo. When Sirianni was asked specifically about Mannion’s responsibility for the offense’s problems, he said no coach or player is on an island. Yet when Sirianni dismissed an offensive coordinator who had been with him for five playoff-bound years, none of which included a four-game losing streak like the Eagles’ current quagmire, he said the plan was a dramatic offensive shift that could provide a better schematic advantage. There’s been no advantage. The scheme inspires little consistent confidence beyond occasional spurts, even though team captain Jordan Mailata said he’s still confident in it.

Eagles’ persistent offensive struggles mean ‘everything’s on the table’ — and that could include Sean Mannion’s role – Inquirer

Sirianni certainly bears culpability for the losing streak. The seeds of his core beliefs, however, don’t provide shade for areas in which his previous ingenuity is now lacking. And that goes to the very root of the Sirianni conundrum. If he can’t devise an offense and/or call plays, and thus has to rely on Mannion-types for innovation, what is his greater value? To save himself, he may need to take back full ownership. It’s been that ugly on offense. Mannion and new offensive line coach Chris Kuper have had almost no solutions for defenses that blitz Eagles quarterbacks when they’re under center and drop to throw. Maybe because they almost always try to run play action in those situations.

Brandon Graham Thought Kellen Moore Could Replace Nick Sirianni After the Super Bowl Win – Crossing Broad

Is it me, or does BG basically admit that the Eagles planned on replacing Nick with Kellen Moore in 2024? That’s how it feels, doesn’t it? Where else would BG get this idea? I feel like the Kellen-Nick switch must’ve been talked about a bunch inside the organization for him to have this theory. Or maybe not. (Kinkead: BG was probably listening to too much WIP) Maybe BG cooked this up on his own. That’s possible. Maybe he — and the rest of the players — saw that Nick didn’t contribute to play-calling at all, and figured that since Kellen Moore was so good at it, he’d be an easy replacement for Nick if things went sideways. Whatever the case may be, it seems like the Eagles winning the Super Bowl in 2024 derailed that plan. Firing Nick after a Super Bowl win would’ve been nearly impossible (but it would’ve been baller as hell… bold move… scared money don’t make money, etc…), and Kellen was bound to move on to a head coaching job after his stellar season calling plays. But still, it’s a fascinating sliding doors moment.

Another Bad Day – Iggles Blitz

Some fans are now screaming for Nick Sirianni’s head. That’s not going to happen this season, nor should it. Firing him would not make this team better. It would just give angry fans something to be happy about. His future will be decided by his overall performance this season. If the offense continues to be the worst in the league, that could very well cost Sirianni his job. If the team shows some improvement and wins some games, that could change things. We need a full season to make an informed evaluation. The next three games are DAL, WAS, and the NYG. The Eagles could be atop the division if they can cobble together a winning streak. Or they could end up closer to a Top 5 pick if they keep losing. Cheer for the outcome you prefer.

2026 NFL season, Week 6: What We Learned from Sunday’s games – NFL.com

McKee struggles early in first meaningful start. The Eagles’ defense kept Philadelphia in the game early, getting off the field in the first half. The defense, however, was gassed late and put in a situation where it needed to be perfect due to the offensive injuries. Tanner McKee, making his first start outside of Week 18, was off the mark something bad early. The QB was blasted on his first snap and nearly threw a pick on the next. McKee’s ball placement wasn’t very good, particularly through the first three quarters. NFL starters can’t miss windows as badly as he did Sunday. Predictably, McKee struggled against pressure behind a shuffled offensive line, going 6 of 15 for 63 yards and a 52.9 rating under pressure, per NGS. Absent a trio of running backs, the ground game was of no help Sunday. Philly rushed for 35 total yards with a Dameon Pierce TD. McKee finished 26 of 45 for 215 yards and a TD, with three sacks. Late, the quarterback did find a groove when he essentially decided to force-feed DeVonta Smith. In the fourth quarter, Smith generated five catches for 53 yards and a TD (7/75/1 for the game). With Jalen Hurts on injured reserve, the Eagles must hope McKee builds on his late-game play. Otherwise, the spiral will continue.

Fantasy football waiver wire targets: NFL Week 7 – PFF

Tanner McKee, Philadelphia Eagles (2.6%). Jalen Hurts is on injured reserve, leaving McKee as Philadelphia’s starter. He threw 45 times in his first start of the season, completing 26 passes for 215 yards and a touchdown. He didn’t have Saquon Barkley at running back to help him, and his wide receivers dealt with injuries during the game. Ideally, Barkley will be back and the receivers will be healthier this week. That’s because the Eagles are playing their division rival, the Dallas Cowboys. The Cowboys have been an excellent matchup for fantasy quarterbacks because their offense scores a lot, forcing opposing quarterbacks to throw frequently to keep up. Their defense has also been among the league leaders in points allowed. If you’re in a deeper league with only a few quarterback options available on the waiver wire, McKee could be the best choice.

Albert Breer’s Week 6 NFL Takeaways: Why You Should Still Trust Howie Roseman and the Eagles – SI

This is where I’d stop and say the Eagles should have your trust. Few have drafted as well as GM Howie Roseman over the past decade. The team’s player development program is as detailed, involved and invested in as any in the league. That’s allowed them to harvest high picks like Johnson, Dickerson, Jurgens, Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean, just as they do diamonds in the rough like Moro Ojomo, Jordan Mailata, Willie Lampkin and Drew Kendall. The thing now is that you’re seeing the core of the title-contending team of the first iteration of the Nick Sirianni era age out, which is leading to those big-picture questions. Where does the team stand on Jalen Hurts as he gets to the end of the guarantees in the megadeal he signed in early 2023? How will the offensive line be retooled, with Johnson and Jurgens gone, and can Lampkin, Kendall and rookie Markel Bell be answers to that? What, for that matter, is the future of the defense, with Mitchell and DeJean likely looking for new deals in 2027, and DC Vic Fangio contemplating retirement? Would a team that’s been aggressive in pulling the plug sooner than later on head coaches consider Sirianni’s future?

Spadaro: What can Tanner McKee, offense learn from Sunday? – PhiladelphiaEagles.com

And that is the theme here: What can the Eagles build on for the next week and the week after that? It starts at the quarterback position with McKee, who has played well in the limited time he’s been on the field – in two Week 18 starts and in a backup role in the 2024 season win over Dallas. “First thoughts, my team needs me to be better,” McKee said after the game. “I need to be better. I am so much better and I’m looking forward to learning everything and becoming the player that I know I am, the player that I can prove that I am. A lot of things that were frustrating that fall on me and a lot of things we gotta get fixed as an offense for sure.” McKee cited areas that he needs to fix – poor communication, placement of players, settling down faster – “making adjustments on the fly.”

If Commanders lose, NFC East will be first division with zero wins in back-to-back weeks since merger – PFT

Thanks to another rough Sunday around the NFC East, the Commanders could make some history on Monday night. Josh Dubow of the Associated Press points out that a Commanders loss to the 49ers at Levi’s Stadium would make the NFC East the first division since the AFL-NFL merger to win zero games over back-to-back weeks despite having all of its teams in action.

The Optimist: An ugly win is still a win – Cat Scratch Reader

I don’t remember the last time the Carolina Panthers played a game this ugly and won. The final 25-14 score belies the fact that it was a one possession game deep in the fourth quarter. A bad snap on 1st & 10 for the Eagles and followed by the secondary losing Tommy Tremble for a 19-yard touchdown pass just seven plays later decided the game with 6:38 seconds left. In the end, the Panthers’ depleted defense barely managed to hold on against an even more depleted Philadelphia Eagles offense. Their offense played a worse game with Taylor Moton and Jalen Coker back on the field than they did against the Detroit Lions without either of them. Bryce Young was fine, but far from the cool, collected star against pressure that he has been most of the season. Ultimately, this is a team with many, well exposed flaws that is sitting at 3-2 with a division game against a reeling Tampa Bay Buccaneers squad next week that could turn their sole lead in the division into an awkward tie with the Saints or a commanding lead. It wasn’t a perfect win, but it was a win.

Falcons sign QB Andy Dalton and release Cooper Rush – The Falcoholic

The Atlanta Falcons, fresh off a loss against the Chicago Bears, are signing veteran quarterback Andy Dalton. In a corresponding move, they’ve cut ties with fellow red-headed quarterback Cooper Rush. To say this is a bit of a curious move would be an understatement, given that Dalton will open up as the third quarterback on the roster. Whether this is the Falcons covering themselves with Michael Penix Jr. getting banged up repeatedly and not wanting to chance Rush getting back into a game in case of a rash of injuries that takes down Penix and backup Tua Tagovailoa, or whether they view Dalton as a possible QB2 over Tua remains to be seen. Either way, Dalton’s a slam dunk upgrade on what the team had with Rush, at the very least.

10 things we learned from Patriots vs. Jets – Pats Pulpit

A.J. Brown has to knock off the rust. The Patriots finally got A.J. Brown back from his four-week stint on injured reserve, and he was not good. Despite being targeted 10 times, he only came down with three catches for 27 yards. It was his drops that were really concerning. There was the deep ball where he pulled his arms in too soon; there was the slant that hit him right in the arms that he dropped; there was the touchdown that Drake Maye placed perfectly on his back shoulder but still went through his hands. To cap things off, he also dropped the onside kick attempt at the end of the game, but luckily Eli Raridon jumped on the ball. Yes, it was his first game back and first game in front of the Patriots home crowd, and he probably was excited to be out there and still has to build a rapport with Maye, but his performance on Sunday was unacceptable. Hopefully, he just has to knock the rust off and will be fine moving forward. The team thinks so, at least.

Is it time to let CJGJ go? – Buffalo Rumblings

This is now 2 games where I see all the negativity pointed at the franchise because of one disrespectful player onour team. I believe its time to let this dude go as the Bills are a better franchise to allow someone that behaves like this to share the sideline with the other professionals on our team. I was willing to turn a blinde eye to some of his antics if he was giving us good production on the field but spitting on another player is downright dirty and disrespectful and I believe our team is better than that and should take these 2 weeks to trade for a replacement or find one sitting at home somewhere.

3 ‘things I think’ after a Giant flop against the Saints: Is it J.J. McCarthy time? – Big Blue View

New York Giants fans overwhelmingly believe J.J. McCarthy should be the team’s quarterback beginning this Sunday against the Houston Texans. Eighty-one percent of the 751 voters in our poll think McCarthy should replace Jameis Winston as the starter when the Giants face the Houston Texans this Sunday. Head coach John Harbaugh wasn’t ready to make that decision in his post-game press conference. “I can’t answer that now,” Harbaugh said. “The game just ended ten minutes ago. “It’s not even up for discussion or conversation right now. We’ve got to go back and go to work. I have no problem with Jameis whatsoever. I love the way he competes, I love the way he fights, all those kind of things. He was up and down today for sure, but those things will all be decided not ten minutes after a game.” It is, though, a decision Harbaugh has to make. When the Giants acquired McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings a few weeks ago for a fifth-round pick, it seemed clear Harbaugh would face this decision at some point. I’m sure he knew that, too. I doubt, though, that anyone expected that choice to have to come now.

10 thoughts on the Cowboys loss to the Packers – Blogging The Boys

1) The no-show offense. In a game where the defense put together an admirable effort, the Cowboys’ offense decided to take the night off. They struggled to sustain drives, and when they did put anything together, they blew it by turning the ball over. Dak Prescott was picked off twice, once when he failed to locate a dropping defender, and then another time when CeeDee Lamb fell down. He was picked off later in the game, but a late-hit penalty negated that one. All the offense could muster was 13 points. It was their lowest-scoring outing of the season, beating the previous low of 16 last week. It was a puzzling disappearing act from a group that started the year doing pretty well. 2) Nothing for Dak. The Packers’ defense gave Prescott fits all night long. It was similar to last week against Tampa Bay when he was under duress a lot and everything he threw went into tight coverage. The Packers did a great job in their zone coverage and Dak just wasn’t able to effectively navigate through the traffic. The only stuff he could complete was short as he never found any success downfield. He looked frazzled in the pocket and never found any rhythm.

NFL predictions: Commanders vs 49ers in primetime – Hogs Haven

This game could lead to a lot of possible short- and long-term changes for the Washington Commanders. If they pull off the upset, hope for their season remains due to a weak NFC East. If they lose, the season becomes more bleak, but Dan Quinn likely plays out the string before an offseason of change for the franchise. If they have another embarrassing loss? Anything can happen after that.

Is Commanders coach Dan Quinn’s job in jeopardy after tie with Giants? – ESPN

Quinn has told people this week he still strongly believes in both first-year coordinators, Blough and Daronte Jones. That doesn’t mean Quinn and his staff receive a free pass. As one team source said, the losing would wear out anyone, including Harris. People who have worked for Harris say he separates emotion from his decision-making, but he’s also not immune to feeling a certain way. An ugly loss in San Francisco likely wouldn’t change anything about Quinn’s status, the source said. Still, the Commanders are 6-15-1 since the start of last season and 3-13-1 in their last 17 games. But, for now, they’re not looking at the past. “The sky is not falling right now,” Cosmi said. “We’ve got 70% of our games to go. Put your head down, keep working, learn from your mistakes and push forward. All the opportunity is there to win the division.”

item.title: The 2026 Chicago Bears just had their statement game
item.description: The 2026 Chicago Bears is coming into focus, and they look like a playoff team. @kdthompson5 has more here.
item.content:encoded:
We just got our first glimpse of the real Chicago Bears on Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons.

That statement doesn’t just reflect the fact that Chicago played arguably its most complete game of the season (notwithstanding the defense played by the backups in the fourth quarter) in their 31-23 win.

It’s about who was on the field making that victory happen, and how.

Yes, Caleb Williams was back, showing Bears fans what they were missing during his absence by completing 30 of 36 passes for 305 yards and a touchdown. His perfect 24-of-24 completions on throws from a clean pocket in this game were the best mark by any quarterback since 2018—a testament to both his protection and his accuracy. His clinical operation of the offense helped the Bears possess the ball for more than 40 minutes and build a 31-7 lead at one point.

But that wasn’t all.

Kyler Gordon reminded everyone he’s one of the best nickel corners in the league when healthy, obliterating the Falcons offense for three sacks and forcing fumbles on two of them.

Luther Burden III (eight catches for 95 yards) and Colston Loveland (six catches for 65 yards and a touchdown) had their way with a beleaguered Falcons secondary. Burden, in particular, continues to look like the clear WR1 for this Bears offense and is currently on pace for a 1,000-yard season.

Ozzy Trapilo, against all odds, returned to action after suffering a torn patellar tendon nine months ago—still can’t get over that. Once he gets his legs under him, the 2025 second-round pick might regain his stranglehold on the starting left tackle spot, locking down Caleb Williams’ blind side opposite Darnell Wright.

Rookie Logan Jones got some brief game action in relief of Garrett Bradbury, who has struggled often this season. While it’s no guarantee Jones will be the starter on Thursday night when the Bears face the Patriots, head coach Ben Johnson might be getting the team ready to make the change.

While the Bears are still missing some notable contributors at the moment—Kyle Monangai, Montez Sweat, and TJ Edwards to name a few—this lineup, from the youth movement to missing game-changers like Gordon, is the one that will keep the Bears pushing toward the playoffs for the second year in a row.

Will there be some growing pains along the way, especially for the young players? Probably. Not every defense the Bears face will be as amenable to getting scored on as Atlanta’s, for example. And, as we unfortunately were reminded of on Sunday, injuries are inevitable in this sport. Good health is far from guaranteed.

But the Bears you saw on Sunday in Atlanta? 

That’s a playoff team. The fun part? They’re probably not even close to as good as they can be yet.

item.title: What’s wrong with the Giants’ run game?
item.description: What has gone wrong with the NY Giants running game?
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants run game could best be described, in a word, as “bad”.

A desire to run the ball has been woven into the very DNA of the Giants’ offense. A strong running game has been John Harbaugh’s signature for as long as he’s been a head coach, and he brought in long-time run game guru Greg Roman to design the Giants’ rushing attack.

Harbaugh also brought fullback Patrick Ricard over from Baltimore in free agency and the Giants made a point of drafting the powerful offensive lineman Sisi Mauigoa. The Giants also drafted Malachi Fields, a big-bodied wide receiver with significant blocking upside.

The Giants’ final roster roster is a departure from NFL norms and featured four running backs, four tight ends, a fullback, and just four wide receivers, one of whom has primarily been a returner.

Despite wanting to be a smash-mouth, run-heavy offense with an emphasis on the power run game, the Giants’ run game has degraded with each passing week. They’ve been plagued by turnovers and largely been ineffective on the ground.

In Week 4, the Giants’ backs carried the ball 28 times (Cam Skattebo: 18, Najee Harris 9, Tyrone Tracy 1), and averaged a combined 3.1 yards per carry with a fumble. In Week 5, the three backs carried the ball 21 times (Skattebo: 13, Harris: 5, Tracy: 3) and averaged 3.5 yards per carry. That, however drops down to just 2.55 yards per carry if we subtract Skattebo’s 19-yard carry at the end of the game as an outlier.

The Giants’ running game reached a new low in the loss to the New Orleans Saints. Harris got the start while Skattebo was (effectively) benched after he fumbled away the game against the Cardinals, getting just six offensive snaps and zero touches.

“I didn’t expect to have zero, but I mean, I was expecting to not play as much just like I did,” Skattebo said after the game. “And the message is keep your head down and keep going, you know. They understand the type of player I am and I just got to continue to do my job and do it to the best of my ability.”

“It sucks, but I can’t put the blame on anybody else but myself,” he added. “I did it to myself. So their consequences leave me on the sidelines, keep me there, and I understand why, like I said. And, I’m going to continue to go out there and give it everything I have for the New York Giants and continue to work hard.”

The Giants running backs carried the ball just 14 times (Tracy: 6, Singletary: 4, Harris: 4) and picked up a total of 34 yards on the ground, for an average of 2.4 yards per carry. Tracy, though, did score the Giants’ first rushing touchdown since Week 1.

After the game, Harbaugh blamed the flow of the game both for the lack of touches as well as Skattebo’s absence. And it is true that the Giants were forced away from the run game once the wheels fell off the offense and defense in the third quarter. However, that also doesn’t explain why the run game was so ineffective when the game was still close or after the Giants had closed the gap.

The problem is multifaceted, with problems in the blocking, the runners, and in the structure of the offense.

Blocking woes

The Giants have struggled to block their run plays. There have been both poor blocks allowing penetration into the backfield as well as free runners that might have been missed blocks or oversights in the blocking scheme.

Harris’ first run of the afternoon might be one such play.

The Giants run a counter play outside zone to the offensive right, while having Darnell Mooney pull to the play-side as a misdirection along with Isaiah Likely from an H-back alignment. The offensive line does a pretty good job of washing most of the Saints’ front to the side and creating an initial lane for Harris. However, Andrew Thomas doesn’t get to the second level, leaving a linebacker to tackle Harris. At the same time, while Chase Young is frozen by Mooney and Likely’s motion, he’s completely unblocked on the back side of the play.

If the Giants intended the motion to freeze the back-side defender long enough for the runner to get to the second level, that would be an issue with the play design. However, if one of Likely and Mooney was supposed to chip Young (which should be Likely), that would be a missed assignment.

On the second play, the Giants call an off-tackle run to the right using outside-zone blocking. Again, it’s initially blocked up well, however the key block falls to tight end Thomas Fidone II, who’s asked to pull from the left edge all the way around to the right side. Fidone does a good job of getting in position, but misses the block.

Harris does a better job than anticipated of getting to the edge, and the Giants had blockers in place at the second level. Both right tackle Marcus Mbow and right guard Sisi Mauigoa did a good job of getting into space and staying ahead of the play. They were in position to block Harris up for a nice run along the right sideline. However, the player Fidone missed was able to torpedo Harris and trip him up for a gain of just 2 yards.

The first play of the very next drive featured an even worse non-block (again from Runyan Jr.).

The Giants once again seek to start the drive with a run, showing a heavy look with both Patrick Rickard at H-back and Isaiah Likely at fullback. Harris takes the handoff, however Runyan is beaten badly by the defensive tackle and driven deep into the backfield and into Harris. The defensive tackle not only takes half-man leverage, but Runyan pops upright out of his stance and never manages to establish any kind of leverage himself. So instead of being able to redirect or re-anchor, he is put on skates.

The running backs

In addition to the blocking issues, the Giants’ backs were also inefficient, and both Harris and Tracy potentially left significant yardage on the field.

“Nobody has really taken the bull by the horns,” Harbaugh said after the game. “Motor (RB Devin Singletary) really hasn’t had a chance to take the bull by the horns. So, we thought we’d get him in the mix, too. So, we put four guys up and see if we can get something going with the running game. That was the idea.

“You can say, well, I don’t like that. I don’t like you divvying up the snaps between four backs. And I can tell you, I don’t like it either,” he added. “One of those guys needs to step up. Somebody needs to step up and be the back. And none of those guys have done that yet. And when one of those guys steps up to be the back, then they’ll be the back. That’s your answer. And that’s as honest as I can be about it. And they know that, too. And believe me, they’re all hungry. They want to step up. One of those guys wants to step up. Somebody’s going to step up and take that job. We’re going to see who it is.”

That was born out in NextGenStats GPS tracking tacking data after the game.

Part of the issue goes back to blocking and their teammates not sustaining their blocks after the handoff. However, the Giants’ backs also showed some lack of patience behind the line of scrimmage.

None of the Giants’ backs had enough carries to qualify for NextGenStats rushing leaders stats. However, we do know that Skattebo was sixth in the NFL in “efficiency” last week, and second in time behind the line of scrimmage. Based on those numbers, it seems likely that the Giants’ primary backs have been trying to hit the holes as hard and fast as possible. However, a modicum of patience could help the Giants realize their missing yardage.

Patience and vision are two of the most important traits among running backs, perhaps even more important than raw speed and explosiveness.

While none of the Giants’ backs are true home run hitters, each has the agility and short-area quickness to exploit running lanes. However, both Skattebo and Harris have struggled with patience at times. One of the knocks on Harris coming out of Alabama was that he can play “in a hurry” and not give blocks a chance to be established. Skattebo, meanwhile, has a tendency to seek contact first, which has led to him missing opportunities for yards after contact in favor of the contact itself. His style can be a spark for the offense when it works, but fumbles and leaving yards on the field are both risks.

Tracy and Singletary both show better tempo as runners, and the Giants also have a tendency to use them from more varied formations than with Harris and Skattebo.

Having multiple skill sets and being able to establish a physical tone as well as having more dynamic threats out of the backfield are both important. That said, the Giants should do more to make their rushing offense look the same no matter who is in the game. That means using varied formations with Harris and Skattebo, as well as coaching them to be a bit more patient behind the line of scrimmage, while also allowing Tracy and Singletary to be more physical.

As mentioned above, it appeared as though the Saints had the Giants’ playbook for much of the game, and their personnel usage could have been part of the tells that allowed the Saints to play so quickly.

Tendencies

A week ago we suggested that the Giants may need to adjust the way they think about offense, and that being too strong in their tendencies has been part of the problem since the loss of Jaxson Dart.

To their credit, the Giants did break out of their schematic mold in this game. They used more screens and outside zone plays, as well as throwing out of heavy sets. However, there may have been personnel and alignment tells that are allowing their opponents to play fast.

In that, the Giants’ fourth quarter could be instructive.

J.J. McCarthy’s fourth quarter near-comeback was impressive, and the Giants’ offense was explosive and dynamic with him on the field. And while the Giants couldn’t afford to run the ball much there was a notable difference with McCarthy in the backfield than with Winston.

The biggest difference was the hesitancy with which the Saints’ second level defenders played. Where the Saints’ second level defenders began moving to the point of attack almost immediately with Winston in the game, they were playing much more slowly with McCarthy at quarterback.

It was most notable on Devin Singletary’s 9-yard run early in the fourth quarter.

There is a very noticeable hesitation among the Saints’ linebackers and safeties, with the safeties backpedaling at the start of the play only to have to stick and drive on the ball. Likewise, their linebackers don’t crash downward and instead stay at the second level after the snap, allowing the Giants’ blockers to establish and lock in their blocks.

The threat of the quarterback run game likely affected the Saints’ defense, forcing them to slow down and make sure McCarthy didn’t keep the ball. But the running back alignment is part of this as well.

Note above how Singletary is even with McCarthy.

With Winston on the field in the shotgun formation, the Giants’ backs tend to line up just behind the quarterback on running plays and even (or in front) on passing plays. Even on the toss play to Harris above (the second gif), he lines up just behind Winston. That isn’t uncommon and certainly isn’t unique to the Giants. Runners lining up behind the quarterback gives them an extra step to time the handoff and accelerate toward the line, while lining up even or in front of the quarterback gives them better vision and positioning for pass protection.

Here, the Saints can’t be sure if McCarthy is going to throw the ball, pull it and run, or hand off to Singletary. And that instant of indecision is all the difference.

It’s a subtle change and could make execution a bit more difficult for the quarterback and running back at first, but playing run and pass from the same alignment in shotgun could go a long way toward slowing the defense.

On the flip side, the Giants tend to either call a run or play-action out of the I-formation. And while being under center makes play-action more effective, losing the threat of a drop-back pass can make runs less effective.

Final thoughts

There is a lot wrong with the Giants running game. But perhaps the most frustrating aspect of their dysfunction is that they’re often very close to hitting on all cylinders.

The Giants absolutely need to tighten up their blocking, both in making the blocks in the first place and sustaining them. Likewise, the backs themselves need to be more patient in letting the blocks develop as well as willing to hit holes as well as defenders.

And finally, the coaches need to continue to refine their play design and calling. The Giants’ runs are typically well schemed and give the players the chance to be effective. But as mentioned above, being able to run more plays from similar looks will help the Giants’ offense be less predictable.

Regardless of whether Winston or McCarthy start going forward, being less obvious in running back alignment out of the shotgun — as well as more multiple in using the run and pass out of the I formation — will go a long way in helping to unlock the Giants’ rushing offense. The Giants want to be a smashmouth football team, and they have the pieces to get there, but it’s on everyone to make that happen.

item.title: Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is out for the season after blood clots found in lungs
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts has blood clots in his lungs, the team announced Monday. Multiple media outlets are reporting that the Super Bowl LIX MVP is out for the season.
item.content:encoded:
Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts has blood clots in his lungs and will not be able to participate in football activities while he is being treated, according to a statement released Monday by the team and Hurts’ agent, Nicole Lynn.

Hurts has been diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis and a bilateral pulmonary emboli, the statement said, meaning a blood clot has traveled from his legs to his lungs. While no timeline was given for Hurts’ return to football, multiple media outlets report that the Super Bowl LIX MVP is out for the season.

“He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations,” the Eagles and Lynn said in their statement. “His treatment should only involve anticoagulation [i.e. “blood thinners”]. During this time, he will not be allowed to participate in any contact activities, including football.

Read more:What Super Bowl? Rams look lifeless during humbling loss to Cardinals

“Jalen’s prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery. We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners. In the meantime, he will remain active around the team and continue to condition. More importantly, we anticipate that he will have no long-term effects.”

Hurts injured his calf during an Oct. 4 loss to the Rams, according to a statement by the Eagles on Thursday, but did not inform his team of the injury until four days later. An ultrasound revealed a superficial blood clot, but Hurts was cleared to play Oct. 11 in London against the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Read more:Nick Sirianni expresses remorse for NSFW reaction to sideline hit on Jalen Hurts

A follow-up ultrasound “revealed movement in the small blood clot,” the team said Thursday, and Hurts was held from the following day’s game against the Carolina Panthers “as we determine the appropriate course of treatment.” Two days later, the Eagles announced that Hurts had been placed on injured reserve, meaning he would miss at least four games.

Tanner McKee started at quarterback for the Eagles on Sunday and completed 26 of 45 passes for 215 yards and a touchdown in the 25-14 loss.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Fantasy Football Waiver Wire Week 7: Omar Cooper Jr. and Germie Bernard break out
item.description: Germie Bernard and Omar Cooper Jr. are coming online just in time to save fantasy football teams. They headline the biggest names on the Week 7 waiver wire.
item.content:encoded:
Week 6 gave us a handful of wide receiver breakouts that now headline the best waiver wire adds of the week. Every player in this article is available in at least half of all Yahoo leagues.

Week 6 Stock Up, Stock Down: The young receivers are here
Rivers McCown highlights four fantasy players whose fantasy football stock rose in Week 6 of the NFL season and four whose stock fell.
  • Rivers McCown,

▶ Quarterback

Aaron Rodgers, Steelers

Rodgers is currently the QB14 on the back of the fifth-most pass attempts in the league. He has thrown multiple touchdowns in each of his past four games and the Steelers have the fourth-highest pass rate over expected. Now he gets a date with the Saints in France for Week 7. The Saints currently rank 23rd in EPA per dropback allowed and were just picked apart by J.J. McCarthy.

Michael Penix, Falcons

Penix played three quarters of dreadful football but redeemed himself in the fourth with two touchdowns and a pair of two-point conversions. He finished the day with three passing touchdowns and 225 yards. It was his best fantasy outing of the year but his worst real-life performance. He gets another difficult matchup with the 49ers next week, though it also profiles as another shootout.

J.J. McCarthy, Giants

This is a Superflex-only add, but a rather important one. We don’t yet know who the Giants will start in Week 7. Jameis Winston was pulled for McCarthy late in Week 6 and the former Viking lit the world on fire. He threw for 243 yards, a touchdown, and a two-point conversion in the fourth quarter. It’s the most yards for a quarterback in the fourth quarter since 2020 and the most yards in 11 minutes of play in NFL history. In true desperation mode, McCarthy simply chucked the ball up to his superstars and let them win. His 15.6 aDOT is the highest in a game (min. 20 dropbacks) this year. McCarthy played like prime Winston after the real thing flopped. I suspect he’ll get the start next week. If he plays like this again, McCarthy will be in the streaming conversation going forward.

J.J. finds Isaiah Likely

: FOX pic.twitter.com/0fLSL9TMTV

— New York Giants (@Giants) October 18, 2026

Tanner McKee, Eagles

McKee was dreadful in his first start of the year, throwing for 215 yards and a touchdown on 45 attempts. He ranked 20th out of 27 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback on the week, pending Monday Night Football. Still, the news that Jalen Hurts will be sidelined for the rest of the year means McKee will make several more starts. If you are truly desperate in Superflex leagues, he’s worth an add.

▶ Running Back

Kendre Miller, Saints

Travis Etienne will miss at least one more game while on IR, meaning Kendre Miller will be the Saints’ lead back for another week. He saw 20-of-33 backfield carries in Week 6 and even managed two targets. Miller only went for 72 scoreless yards on his high-volume role, but the touch total was rather impressive for a member of a three-back committee. Miller will have some RB3 life when he takes on the Steelers in a week.

Roschon Johnson, Bears

Johnson has seamlessly stepped in as D’Andre Swift’s backup, getting on the field for exactly 40 percent of the snaps in each of his past two games. Over the past two weeks, Johnson has run a route on 37 percent of Caleb Williams’ dropbacks and is being targeted on 24 percent of those routes. He also snuck in a goal line touchdown on Sunday. His role will evaporate once Kyle Monangai is healthy, but Johnson is a safe bet for a dozen touches per game until that happens.

Bam Knight, Cardinals

Somehow Bam Knight returned. He made eight starts for Arizona last year but began 2026 buried behind Jeremiyah Love and Tyler Allgeier on the depth chart. With Love out for Week 6, the Cardinals simply stuck with a backfield-by-committee, giving Knight 15 carries to Allgeier’s 18. Knight was far more productive, gashing the Rams for 80 yards compared to a measly 38 for Allgeier. Arizona still used Allgeier as the primary option on passing downs, but Knight managed a 40 percent route rate and saw the team’s lone goal line carry. Until Love returns, Knight appears to be the 1B in his backfield.

Jaleel McLaughlin, Browns

McLaughlin and Audric Estime each saw nine carries in Week 6. Estime found the end zone but McLaughlin almost made up for that in PPR formats with four catches. McLaughlin would be a viable RB3/4 for Week 7, but the team should get one or both of Dylan Sampson and Quinshon Judkins back by Sunday. You can add McLaughlin, but the most likely outcome is that he can be cut in a few days.

▶ Wide Receiver

Germie Bernard, Steelers

Rostered in exactly half of all Yahoo leagues as of Sunday night, Bernard qualifies for this article without any caveats and is not a “Not in My League” all-star. Bernard is a perfect fit for Aaron Rodgers, operating as an easy underneath option while creating plenty of extra yards after the catch. He racked up 11 grabs on 12 targets in Week 6 and scored the game-winning touchdown to go long with 87 yards. With Roman Wilson and Michael Pittman both banged up, the second-round pick looks like a weekly WR3. If he’s still out there, Bernard is the player to blow all of your FAAB on.

Omar Cooper Jr., Jets

Cooper was activated off IR over the weekend and immediately looked like the play-making WR2 the Jets hoped they were getting at the end of the first round. The rookie reeled in six catches for 103 yards and a score.

The rookie Omar Cooper Jr. makes the 48-yard touchdown catch!

He also had a touchdown called back via an extremely light offensive pass interference on Tim Patrick. We’re working with an extremely small sample, but Cooper is averaging 4.6 yards per route run while being targeted on 28 percent of his routes. Assuming Bernard isn’t available to you, this is the best waiver wire add of the week. I will be getting down 30-40 percent of my FAAB on Cooper.

Tre Tucker, Raiders

Tucker blew up against a vulnerable Buffalo defense with five catches for 97 yards and a pair of touchdowns. It was his first spike week since Week 2, though he had at least four catches for 40 yards in three straight games between the spikes. Tucker has been a different player in Klint Kubiak’s offense. He is on pace for a career high in yards per route run (1.96) and is posting his best season by PFF receiving grade and ESPN’s Overall Score, which combines their metrics on getting open, catching the ball, and producing YAC. He isn’t a true breakout bet like Cooper or Bernard, but Tucker rounds out a big three at receiver this week.

Keenan Allen, Colts

He is inevitable. Allen totaled 11 targets in Week 6. He caught eight of them for 82 yards. He has at least nine targets in three straight games. Josh Downs hasn’t seen that type of receiving volume since Week 3. The ceiling with Allen is rather limited, and his role will take a hit if Tyler Warren is back from his groin injury next week. On the other hand, he has posted top-20 fantasy numbers in two of his past three starts. He should at least be rostered in most leagues.

Kendrick Bourne, Cardinals

Bourne has taken Marvin Harrison Jr.’s spot in the lineup and is already a more productive WR2 for the Cardinals. He has exactly five catches on eight targets in each of his past two games. Bourne has racked up 117 yards over the past two weeks. Bourne isn’t going to threaten for a breakout season, but he’s not a bad add if you desperately need WR4 points.

Jaylin Noel, Texans

Noel had been percolating under the surface before Week 6 with efficient per-route numbers in a part-time role. He broke out in London with four catches for 107 yards and a touchdown. He’s now averaging over 2.5 yards per route run and is on pace for nearly 1,000 yards. The bad news is that his route rate remained capped at 61 percent in Week 6, meaning the fantasy success wasn’t underpinned by an improved role. Fantasy managers can hope that his role grows, but it's hard to bank on that with Tank Dell set to return and Marvin Harrison Jr. in town.

Jahan Dotson, Falcons

Dotson is quietly stacking games, with at least 50 yards in back-to-back-to-back weeks and two touchdowns over that stretch. His route rate climbed to 92 percent in Week 6. Dotson is more of a threat to Kyle Pitts’ role than the Falcons WR3s are a threat to Dotson. He’s in the FLEX mix for Week 7 against the 49ers.

Keon Coleman, Bills

Coleman has scored in three straight weeks. He has 11 catches for 182 yards over that stretch. DJ Moore left Week 4 early and missed the next two games, meaning Coleman’s production has come in the absence of Buffalo’s WR1. With a bye on tap for Week 7, Moore should be healthy by the next time we see the Bills. That makes Coleman a stash only in rather deep leagues.

Travis Hunter, Jaguars

The Jags get Week 7 off after a two-game road trip to London, so this is a stash for Week 8 and beyond. Hunter finally saw his usage on offense tick up on Sunday, catching four passes for 59 yards and a score. He only ran seven routes, but Brian Thomas Jr. wasn’t far ahead with just 13 routes. Liam Coen benched BTJ in the second half and used Hunter as a part-time wideout. Whether this two-way role finally sticks is anyone’s guess, but there are worse stashes in deep leagues.

▶ Tight End

Michael Mayer, Raiders

Tight end is a true wasteland on waivers. Mayer is technically a backup. In reality, he’s the Raiders’ starting tight end and Brock Bowers is the team’s WR1. Since Bowers returned in Week 3, Mayer has a 67 percent route rate with a 15 target share. He is averaging 11.5 PPR points per game over the past month. Mayer is averaging more fantasy points with Bowers healthy than he was when the star tight end was sidelined.

Darnell Washington, Steelers

Pat Freiermuth was banged up in Week 6, forcing him to split snaps with Washington. The Steelers’ multiple absences at wide receiver, however, put the team in 12-personnel more often, which increased the number of tight end routes up for grabs. Washington, in turn, ran 55 percent of the routes, logged a 14 percent target share, and finished the week as a low-end TE1 on the back of a short touchdown. He’s nothing more than a TE2 flyer for Week 7, but that’s all we’re getting off waivers right now.

item.title: The Rams might already be dead in the water
item.description: Rams likely must go 8-3 in remaining games in order to make the playoffs
item.content:encoded:
At 2-4. the season might already be over for the Los Angeles Rams.

LA may need to win 10 games in order to make the postseason. The playoffs would wipe the slate clean. All it takes it earning a spot in the tournament. The rest is a matter of taking care of business.

But getting there would mean a 8-3 record over the final 11 regular season games.

Why are 10 wins needed? Because the Silver Bulletin is projecting three NFC teams (Rams, Packers, Bears) to finish with a 9-win record. The Rams could reasonably make the playoffs with nine wins, although their chances suddenly come down to factors outside of their control.

The Packers and Bears are also 4-2 currently. Both have battled early season struggles—in Chicago’s case missing Caleb Williams—to bounce back in resounding fashion. The Rams would need to keep pace with these teams and pull ahead by year’s end. That isn’t easy either.

So how likely would 10 wins be? It’s a difficult path.

Week 7 at Las Vegas Raiders

After starting 3-0, the Raiders have dropped three-straight to fall to .500. This is a game the Rams should win, although they were also expected to trounce a 1-4 Cardinals team. We know that didn’t happen. Why should we be optimistic about their chances in Vegas?

Week 10 at Arizona Cardinals

The Rams would likely be favored in a rematch. Assuming Trent McDuffie and Myles Garrett play in this game after missing the first matchup, these changes would seem to favor LA. However, we can’t count this as an automatic win after the Rams just suffered a disappointing loss to this team.

Week 12 vs Green Bay Packers

One of the most non-NFC West games left on the Rams’ schedule. Winning the NFC West is probably out of the picture at this point. LA is instead competing against the likes of the Packers, assuming they don’t win the NFC North and enter the playoffs as a division winner. The Rams will need this game for head-to-head and strength of schedule tiebreakers. In turn, losing this matchup would be catastrophic.

Week 13 vs Kansas City Chiefs

The Chiefs are undefeated at 5-0. Similar to the 49ers, they haven’t really been challenged much yet this season. They have a point differential of 57, which means on average they are winning by more than 10 points per game.

Week 14 at San Francisco 49ers

Getting back on track means the Rams must fare well in their divisional matchups. Three games remaining against the 49ers and Seahawks gives LA upside potential. It also means three contests against formidable foes. We know Week 1 against San Francisco wasn’t particularly close. LA’s injury woes have only gotten worse. Why should we expect a different outcome this time?

Week 16 at Seattle Seahawks

Week 18 vs Seattle Seahawks

The Rams will finish the regular season facing Seattle in two of the last three games. The currently 1-5 Tampa Bay Buccaneers are sandwiched in between.

There is a chance that Seattle already has a playoff berth locked up heading into the season finale. That could benefit the Rams if they choose to rest starters. But if the Seahawks are in full force this will likely be a close game.

item.title: Seahawks vs. Chiefs odds: Yes, the Seahawks are somehow favored over Chiefs
item.description: The Seahawks are slight favorites against the still-undefeated Chiefs.
item.content:encoded:
For the second time in three weeks, an undefeated team is headed to Lumen Field as an underdog.

According to the current line at FanDuel Sportsbook, the 3-3 Seattle Seahawks are 2.5-point (-106) favorites against the 5-0 Kansas City Chiefs (-114). On the moneyline, the Seahawks are priced at -132, with the Chiefs coming back at +112.

On the back of a healthy Patrick Mahomes and former Seahawk Kenneth Walker’s fantastic start to life in Kansas City, the Chiefs have gotten off to a 5-0 start and are firmly back atop the league’s hierarchy.

Seattle, meanwhile, finds itself on a two-game skid after dropping an NFC West clash against the 49ers and a prime-time game to the Denver Broncos in consecutive weeks. Between Kansas City’s revamped, controlling offense and the Seahawks’ struggles on offense, Week 7 sees a relatively low total of 41.5 points on the board.

The Chiefs took the last meeting between these former AFC West rivals, a 24-10 win in 2022. Their last visit to Seattle, however, saw the Seahawks come out on top in a 38-31 thriller in 2018, when Russell Wilson outdueled Patrick Mahomes and Doug Baldwin caught his final NFL touchdown pass.
