item.title: Rams have fallen to fifth-best odds to win the Super Bowl
item.description: The Rams entered the season as overwhelming favorites to win the Super Bowl.
item.content:encoded:
The Rams entered the season as overwhelming favorites to win the Super Bowl. After starting the season 2-4, their odds have fallen.

But they may not have fallen as far as some would expect for a team that just lost at home to the Cardinals: The Rams still have the fifth-best odds to win the Super Bowl, at +1000.

The four teams ahead of the Rams are the 49ers at +580, the Bills at +720, the Chiefs at +850 and the Ravens at +900.

Despite their shockingly bad start to the season, bettors and bookmakers still think the Rams have one of the best rosters in the NFL, with a team that should be playing very good football down the stretch. Making the playoffs is no sure thing after this start, but if the Rams do make it, there's every reason to believe they'll be a tough team to beat.

item.title: Philadelphia Eagles QB Jalen Hurts to miss the the rest of the season
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles QB Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the remainder of the season with blood clots in his lungs
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Eagles will be without quarterback Jalen Hurts for the remainder of the 2026 season, per reports. It is now being reported that tests over the weekend revealed that Hurts has multiple blood clots in his lungs.

Ian Rapoport is reporting that Hurts played in London against the Jacksonville Jaguars without having slept because sleeping was a risk.

That, of course, begs the question of just how much the Eagles’ coaching and medical staffs knew of his condition and why they would allow him to play football if sleeping was too risky.

Despite the fact that Hurts plays for a division rival, our first concern is, of course, for his long-term health. Football is secondary, and he needs to take whatever time and steps necessary to get healthy in this scary situation.

From the perspective of the New York Giants, the loss of Hurts is an opportunity. The Giants may have imploded against the New Orleans Saints and have fallen to 3-2-1 on the season, but they still have a 1.5-game lead in the division after both the Eagles and Dallas Cowboys lost this week.

The Eagles’ season appears to be falling apart around them, and Dallas’ defense is an albatross that only perfect offensive play from Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb can overcome. The Giants absolutely need to tighten up their own offense and stop being their own worst enemies on offense and defense. However, the path is still there to right the ship, complete the “worst to first” jump in a division in turmoil, and win the NFC East.

item.title: Brock Purdy and the 49ers can expect plenty of blitzing from the Commanders
item.description: We take a look at 3 numbers to know between the 49ers and Commanders
item.content:encoded:
Fresh off a huge Week 5 divisional win against the Seattle Seahawks, the San Francisco 49ers begin their longest stretch of games without an NFC West opponent with a Monday night date against the Washington Commanders.

Washington has already aided the 49ers this season, handing Seattle its first loss of the season with a Week 3 win over San Francisco’s division rival. A Commanders loss to the 49ers on Monday night would also be a huge boost for San Francisco, with a win putting the 49ers up three games in the NFC West. 

The 49ers will look to avoid a letdown spot against a lesser Washington team. Here are the numbers to know heading into the Monday night clash: 

37.7

Percent. The Commanders blitz on 37.7 of opponents’ dropbacks, the second-highest rate in the league.

The dam finally broke for the 49ers offense when Seattle’s defense got to Brock Purdy for the first three sacks San Francisco has allowed this season. The 49ers offense will now have to face the team that sends an extra man or two at the second-highest clip in the league on Monday night.

Unfortunately, that high blitz rate hasn’t done much for the lacking Washington pass defense.

Because of the blitz, Washington’s defense ranks well in pressure rate (9th) and hurry percentage (6th), but that hasn’t resulted in sacks. Washington ranks 24th with nine sacks, and since the pass rush can’t bring down the opposing quarterback, the Commanders’ poor secondary has been exposed to the tune of:

  • 255 passing yards per game (4th-highest)
  • 14 passing touchdowns (tied for most)
  • 67 passing first downs (third-most)

Purdy’s been in incredible form to start the season, and that form should continue against the lacking Washington secondary, so long as the San Francisco offense can handle the blitzes that Dan Quinn and his Washington defense will present.

67.7

Rushing yards per game. Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels averages 67.7 rushing yards per game.

With Washington’s leading rusher Jacory Croskey-Merritt (groin) out on Monday night, the onus will be on Daniels to pick up the slack in the run game, something he’ll have no issue in taking on.

Entering Week 6, Daniels ranked eighth among quarterbacks with 21 rush attempts. The only reason he doesn’t have more is the two games he missed, but despite the missed games, Daniels 203 rushing yards are second-most for quarterbacks behind only Josh Allen, who has 239 rushing yards on twice as many rush attempts in his five games.

Simply put, the 49ers will not face a more prolific mobile quarterback this season than Daniels.

Raheem Morris and the 49ers defense have faced one quarterback with more rush attempts so far this season than Daniels, and that was Malik Willis in Week 2 when the 49ers beat the Miami Dolphins.

Willis is a quality rusher in his own right, with the third-most at the position, 186 rushing yards on his 27 rush attempts. His 6.9 yards per attempt rank fourth among quarterbacks with 15 or more rushing attempts this season. But when the 49ers faced him, Willis couldn’t get his legs going, holding the quarterback to a season-low six rushing yards on two carries.

Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough will draw up at least two designed runs for Daniels, so don’t expect a Willis-like ground usage for Washington’s quarterback on Monday night.

4

Times. The 49ers have started 6-0 four times in franchise history (1948, 1984, 1990, and 2019).

A win on Monday night would mark the fifth time the 49ers have started the first third of the season without a loss. Each of the last three 6-0 starts have meant at least an NFC Championship Game appearance (in the Super Bowl era).

1948 was the only 6-0 start in 49ers history that didn’t result in a playoff game appearance (the 14-0 Cleveland Browns claimed the 1948 AAFC Championship defeating the Buffalo Bills), but the 49ers would finish 12-2. Those 12 wins came against teams like the New York Yankees, Brooklyn Dodgers, Los Angeles Dons, and Chicago Rockets.

But since the invention of the Super Bowl, a 6-0 start has meant at least an NFC Championship Game appearance for the 49ers. The 2026 49ers have the chance to do something the 1984 team did: go 6-0 with a Monday night win against an NFC East foe. 1984 saw the 49ers defeat the New York Giants to move to 6-0 with a 31-10 Monday Night Football win. San Francisco’s quest for perfection in 1984 would end the next week with a loss against Pittsburgh, but the 49ers would go on to win the franchise’s second Super Bowl.

The 1990 49ers would use a Week 6 win against the Steelers to move to 6-0. The streak would continue into the middle of November when a Week 12 loss to the Rams would drop San Francisco to 10-1. San Francisco would finish 1990 with a 14-2 record but fall short in the NFC Championship Game to a 13-3 Giants team that would go on to win Super Bowl XXV.

The most recent 6-0 team was Kyle Shanahan’s third season with the 49ers in 2019, when San Francisco moved to 6-0 with a sloppy 9-0 win in a rainy Washington, D.C. The 49ers would stay undefeated a few more weeks before losing to Seattle to end the start-of-the-season winning streak at eight games. The 49ers would again make the Super Bowl, but fell to the Chiefs in Miami.

Now, 6-0 doesn’t guarantee postseason success, but the history shines brightly on the 2026 49ers’ Monday night win.

item.title: Colts fire general manager Chris Ballard
item.description: It’s a bad day for the rest of the AFC South
item.content:encoded:
Well, if you lose at home to the Tennessee Titans, someone has to get fired. Today, that someone was Indianapolis Colts general manager Chris Ballard. This move was really a long time coming. Ballard has been doing a pretty terrible job with the Colts for years. I hoped they would keep him forever.

Ballard didn’t just get fired because he sent two first-round picks to the New York Jets for CB Sauce Gardner, but that certainly didn’t help. If you are going to trade two first-round picks for a player, especially a defensive player, that player better be a game wrecker. Gardner is a really good player, but that was a huge overpay.

Colts fans probably think it can’t get any worse than Ballard. Speaking as a Titans fan, it can always get worse. Here’s to hoping whoever the Colts hire is even worse than Ballard, and they go into the same downward spiral the Titans have been in these last few years. They deserve it after getting Peyton Manning and Andrew Luck back-to-back.

item.title: Aaron Glenn: No confusion about who got the ball to start the second half
item.description: Jets head coach Aaron Glenn's on-field interview before the start of the second half on Sunday went viral, but Glenn said on Monday that his comments were misinterpreted.
item.content:encoded:
Jets head coach Aaron Glenn's on-field interview before the start of the second half on Sunday went viral, but Glenn said on Monday that his comments were misinterpreted.

Glenn told Aditi Kinkhabwala of CBS that the team would be ready to go despite being down 17-3 and that "the good thing is we get the ball, we get a chance to go move it and finish." That was widely interpreted to be Glenn saying that the Jets would receive the kickoff to start the second half, which was not the case, and Glenn said on Monday that he was talking about what would happen after the defense forced a stop.

“No, I actually talked about just the offense,” Glenn said on Monday, via Howie Kussoy of the New York Post. “I think they were talking about sustaining drives, and my conversation with them is when the offense gets the ball back, man, we want to be able to sustain a drive and go score. Then when the defense gets back on, we want to make sure we stop them and get the ball back to our offense. That’s what I was talking about when it comes to that. The conversation was talking about the offense at that time.”

Things actually did work out as Glenn hoped as the Jets forced a punt and then scored on a touchdown pass to rookie wideout Omar Cooper. They would eventually pull within 17-13, but the Patriots went on to win 26-19.

item.title: Six Other Heroes From BYU’s Momentous Win Over Notre Dame
item.description: We all know the name Bear Bachmeier. If, by some miracle, Bachmeier were to become the second ever Heisman Trophy winner in BYU history or at least get invited to the ceremony, the path to that moment truly gained traction against the Fighting Irish on Saturday night. He was clearly the biggest hero from the […]
item.content:encoded:
We all know the name Bear Bachmeier. If, by some miracle, Bachmeier were to become the second ever Heisman Trophy winner in BYU history or at least get invited to the ceremony, the path to that moment truly gained traction against the Fighting Irish on Saturday night. He was clearly the biggest hero from the 28-24 win by No. 8 BYU over No. 2 Notre Dame. Per Kirk Herbstreit on X, “(Bachmeier is) the FIRST FBS player in the past 30 years to throw, catch, and rush for TD against an AP TOP 5 opponent in the same game.”

He deserves all the praise and possible accolades that come with that special win and so far, special season for Bachmeier and BYU. But this is a moment to allow others into the spotlight. Let’s highlight six other players who played a massive role in BYU upsetting the Irish in the biggest win at LaVell Edwards Stadium maybe ever.

Preston Rex, RB

What if I told you that BYU would out-gain Notre Dame on the ground without reigning Big 12 Offensive Player of the Year LJ Martin at running back? I would have been checked for signs of hallucinations or hypnosis. BYU did exactly that. Credit to offensive coordinator Aaron Roderick for getting creative. Of course, Bachmeier did his portion on the ground with 44 yards on 14 attempts and two touchdowns. But Rex needs his flowers. Most discounted the run game outside of Bachmeier against this vaunted Irish run defense. Instead, Rex averaged 6.6 yards per carry on 10 totes for 66 yards. He had two runs of at least 10 yards and gained three first downs. He provided enough of a variety in the run game for the Irish to have to think about someone other than Bear.

Kyler Kasper, WR

I almost listed Kasper as “WR/QB.” The double pass from Bachmeier to Kasper, who tossed it back to Bachmeier for a touchdown, was a thing of beauty. Not only was that a dime of a pass from a 6-foot-6 receiver, but Kasper was a huge player in the passing attack at his traditional receiver role as well. Getting eight targets, he hauled in six passes for 66 yards. He was clearly Bachmeier’s most reliable weapon in key spots as four of his six catches earned first downs. His passing touchdown combined with his skills as the tall receiver option for Bachmeier earned himself kudos here. What a pickup for Kalani Sitake, getting Kasper from Oregon in the transfer portal.

Bruce Mitchell, C

The offensive line never gets the love they deserve. All-Big 12 center Bruce Mitchell played one of his finest games as a Cougar. Per Pro Football Focus, Mitchell was BYU’s highest graded offensive lineman in the winning effort. in 38 pass blocking snaps, he didn’t even allow a single quarterback pressure, let alone sack or hit. He had a perfect day at the office in pass protection. He also provided a key block to spring Bachmeier free after he caught the double pass from Kasper. Mitchell’s block after getting to the outside gave Bachmeier a lane to run into the endzone.

Cade Uluave, LB

Uluave was BYU’s most important transfer this offseason. After earning All-ACC honors at Cal, Uluave came to Provo to essentially replace Jack Kelly, now in the NFL. He hasn’t just replaced Kelly on the field. He has been one of the biggest veteran leaders and most important locker room pieces for Sitake as well. All that was on display on Saturday night. He collected nine tackles, which led the team. He added a tackle for loss as well. He wasn’t just your typical off-ball linebacker either. He was BYU’s most effective pass rusher as well, leading the team with five QB pressures. He was everywhere, flying sideline-to-sideline.

Isaiah Glasker, LB

BYU might have the best linebacker duo in at least the Big 12 Conference with Uluave and Glasker. Glasker got hurt against TCU and missed the game against Iowa State. His status for the game was in doubt during the week. He played and made an enormous impact. He ended up being BYU’s highest graded defender per PFF. With six tackles and three pass breakups, Glasker was a menace.

Raider Damuni, S

Getting Damuni back from injury after he got hurt against Utah Tech was a huge boost to the defense. He didn’t miss a beat. In fact, he looked better than ever. Pro Football Focus has a stat called “stops” which is described as “ tackles that constitute a ‘failure’ for the offense.” Damuni led the team with six stops. That is twice as many as the next closest BYU defender. In coverage, he faced six targets from Notre Dame’s talented quarterback, CJ Carr. Damuni allowed just three catches in those six passes, totaling in a meager 12 yards for the Irish. Damuni was a big reason why the Notre Dame passing offense was limited for much of the game. He held their talented wideout  Micah Gilbert to zero catches when the two were matched up, including Damuni’s lone pass breakup.

item.title: The Cleveland Browns are good. What do we all do now?
item.description: At 4-2, the Browns are in first place in their division, a spot they haven't been in this late in a season since 2014.
item.content:encoded:
There are certain truths we hold to be self-evident: The sun rises in the east. Star Wars movies were better when you were a kid. And the Cleveland Browns will always, always be terrible. 

So what happens when one of our bedrock truths turns out to be wrong? What happens when — I can’t believe I’m writing this — the Cleveland Browns turn out to be good? 

As of Week 6, the Cleveland Browns lead the AFC North — by tiebreaker, at least — with a record of 4-2. That’s better than the defending champion Seahawks, better than the supposed super-team Rams, better than the entire NFC South and East. This is the latest the Browns have been in first place in a season since 2014, one of those stats that makes you cringe because it even has to be said. 

How did this happen? Well, nobody’s going to like the answer. Coming into the season, the verdict on Cleveland was that this was a donut of a team, blessed with talent on both sides of the ball but lacking that essential core — i.e., a quarterback. This problem has haunted Cleveland for decades, of course, but it became particularly acute when Cleveland’s front office piled up draft picks and then, shockingly, used them wisely. 

Shedeur Sanders wasn’t the one. Dillon Gabriel wasn’t the one. Joe Flacco wasn’t the one. As it turned out, the one quarterback able to lead the Cleveland Browns to victory is the quarterback nobody wants to lead the Cleveland Browns to victory. 

Deshaun Watson, it turns out, is the answer to Cleveland’s quarterback troubles. Of course. 

Watson, who’s been accused of dozens of counts of sexual assault and settled 20 claims, is just about the last person any organization would want as the face of their team. Were this virtually any other workplace, Watson would have been kicked to the curb and forgotten years ago. But the NFL has a forgiveness blind spot for players who are just too talented to disregard, and Watson has set up camp in that blind spot. 

Regardless of the court of public opinion — and the Browns, among other teams, made it clear they don’t recognize the authority of that court when they pursued Watson in the first place — Watson has met all the terms of his employment with the NFL. That means all his past “adversity” — the euphemism announcers are now employing to sanitize the many allegations against him — will remain in his past. And as distasteful as it may be to a swath of NFL fans, Watson is forcing the league to consider him in football terms, not social ones. 

From a football standpoint, Watson has been a qualified success this season. He’s not dominating games, but he’s not losing them, either, which in the current NFL is enough. He has seven touchdowns against two interceptions this season, with a passer rating of 92.0 and a completion rate of 63.8 percent. That’s not good enough to reign, but it’s good enough to survive. 

The Browns are coalescing around Watson. The defense lost Myles Garrett via trade, but remains strong enough to contain opposing offenses. Against Baltimore on Sunday, for instance, Cleveland’s defense gave up 10 points in the first quarter, but nothing the rest of the game. That allowed Watson and the offense to plod along, turning a crucial Derrick Henry fumble into a touchdown and kicking just two field goals, including a walkoff game-winner. 

The Browns are reveling in the moment … for the moment. “I’m going to enjoy tonight,” first-year head coach Todd Monken said after the win. “And that’s what you have to do in the NFL. These are the nights that you don’t ever want to end, because tomorrow it’s on to the next game.”

Here’s the good news for Cleveland: the “next game” is woeful Tennessee. After that, the Steelers, the Saints, the Texans — on and on, winnable game after winnable game. The only current division leader on the Browns’ remaining schedule: the NFC East’s Giants. Not exactly a fearsome slate. 

This most definitely isn’t the way you want to build a team, with a radioactive quarterback and a defense that relies more on opportunity than overwhelming force. But it’s working for Cleveland, and in a year where there’s no one dominant team, slow and steady keeps you in the race. 

No, we’re not saying the Cleveland Browns will go 15-2 this season. But we’re saying there’s a non-zero chance they could. And that should concern all of us. Because if the Cleveland Browns are now good, what can we even believe in anymore?

item.title: Steelers PFF grades: Germie Bernard shines; Troy Fautanu stagnates
item.description: If cornerback Jamel Dean can stay healthy, he may be a rare veteran acquisition to work out for the Pittsburgh Steelers at the position.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers erased a 16-3 fourth-quarter deficit to beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 26-19 in overtime Oct. 18. 

The comeback was fueled by a defense that started forcing Tampa Bay quarterback Jalon Daniels into costly mistakes, along with a passing game that overcame an ugly first half in which quarterback Aaron Rodgers and Co. could not move the ball with any consistency. 

Here’s a look at some notable numbers from the outing via Pro Football Focus, the scouting website for whom evaluators grade players for every snap of every game on a 1-100 scale.

Required reading: Steelers win first 'Tomlin game' of the Mike McCarthy era with comeback

Germie Bernard (67.7) 

The thing that stands out most from the rookie’s career-best performance of 11 catches for 87 yards and the game-winning touchdown against Tampa Bay is how much of it was in his hands. Literally. Bernard’s average depth of target (ADOT) for the day was a miniscule 1.8 yards. On average, that shouldn’t translate to much production at all, because it puts the onus on the receiver to gain meaningful yardage after the catch. Bernard managed to pick it up in chunks all day, though, to finish with a YAC total of 68. The Steelers would probably prefer for him to become more of a downfield threat – his ADOT of 5.1 yards is a major reason his season grade is a pedestrian 61.2. If he can continue to build chemistry with Rodgers, however, he could be a valuable weapon in this Mike McCarthy offense that is increasingly leaning on short, quick passes. 

Cam Heyward (85.8) 

The 37-year-old got off to a slower start than we’re used to with just five pressures in the first three games of 2026. He also had just three stops – defined by PFF as plays that result in failure for the opposing offense – in that span. In the past three games, however, he’s turned it on with 11 pressures, five stops and two performances graded at 85.8 or better. Heyward has finished with a season grade of at least 84.4 in eight of the past nine seasons, so he’s taking major steps back toward the level of dominance that may some day lift him to the Pro Football Hall of Fame. If there’s a lingering concern, it’s that Heyward hasn’t found a way to get home against opposing quarterbacks nearly as often yet. He has just one sack so far, putting him on pace for three over the course of the season. That would be his lowest output ever over a fully healthy season in which he held a starting role throughout. 

Troy Fautanu (66.5 season grade) 

Four more pressures allowed against Tampa Bay, including a sack and quarterback hit on Rodgers, brought the third-year tackle’s total to 17 this season. Only 11 tackles league-wide have allowed more. Granted, only two tackles have taken more pass blocking snaps, so some of that leakiness is a product of the pure volume of passing that coach Mike McCarthy’s offense is doing right now. Still, Fautanu hasn’t taken that next step toward being a cornerstone as the Steelers hoped he might be when they invested a first-round NFL draft pick in him back in 2024. That’s especially true when you consider that his pass blocking grade of 69.6 is well ahead of his run blocking grade of 57.7. He’s shown virtually no growth in either category since his rookie season. He’s less volatile than former teammate and 2023 first rounder Broderick Jones was, but it’s hard to see the upside that matches the draft capital used to acquire him right now. Rookie Max Iheanachor (68.9) is already grading better. 

Jamel Dean (84.9) 

The Steelers have had a major problem getting production from veteran cornerbacks they’ve signed or traded for in recent years. From Patrick Peterson to Steven Nelson to Donte Jackson to Darius Slay last season, they’ve been ordinary at best and flat-out bad at worst after joining the team. Dean’s trajectory wasn’t promising either before Sunday. He’d missed most of two of the previous three games with an injury and was picked on by Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow in the third. It wasn’t what the Steelers hoped for when they signed him to a three-year, $36.7 million contract in March. He rose to the occasion against Tampa Bay, though. It wasn’t just his interception that set up the game-tying field goal in the fourth quarter. Daniels tested Dean in his return from injury with 11 targets on the afternoon. He allowed just four catches for 48 yards on those plays and permitted just five yards after the catch. It was a great outing that lifted his season grade to a very solid 86.2. If he can stay healthy, he may be the veteran to break the front office’s streak of bad luck at this position. 

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Steelers PFF grades: Germie Bernard shines; Troy Fautanu stagnates

item.title: UNC beats Duke — Winners, Losers, & Honorable Mentions
item.description: It was way harder than it had to be, but it was still a big win
item.content:encoded:
It didn’t need to be that hard.

Carolina fans had seen this story before: the quick 17-0 lead on the road, a sinking feeling of when things would start to crash, and then the torture of the lead disappearing. The first sign was an unfortunate fumble, and yet the defense just kept giving the Tar Heels chances to run away with it. The offense couldn’t convert, and then special teams just seemed to make the inevitable happen.

Then a funny thing happened — the offense came back to life just in the nick of time. Once again, the Tar Heels didn’t completely fold, and between a game-winning drive and a great interception, Carolina rode back to Chapel Hill with the Victory Bell for the first time in a couple of years.

So let’s dive right into the winners, losers, and honorable mentions for UNC’s 24-20 win over the Blue Devils.

Winners

Jaylen McGill – One huge problem for the UNC offense was how early Benjamin Hall went down. Hall was trying to stretch out a play and basically got pulled in opposite directions on the tackle. All of a sudden, Carolina’s deep running back corps suffered a huge hit. McGill took some time to get warmed up, but he’s someone that the staff has had their eyes on. On the last drive, though, he had his signature moments. On a fourth and four he rushed for 16 to keep things moving, and then right out of the two minute timeout he took the ball and scampered 24 yards for the go-ahead score. That he was able to not only extend the drive but win the game turned what could have been a disaster for Carolina into arguably the biggest win of the Belichick Era.

Jordan Shipp – As amazing as he’s been for Carolina this year, it took into the sixth game for him to finally get a touchdown. What he had to do to actually get that touchdown will have that clip being shown when his name is called in the NFL Draft. It’s one thing to make some hay as a receiver when you have a great quarterback, but it’s another when you take — we’ll call them rough — passes and haul them in for scores. Even his mistake is one that comes with a silver lining. When Shipp fumbled on the play that led to Duke’s first score, instead of yelling at teammates or an official, he just walked to the sideline with his head up and tapped himself on the chest, raising his hand to say “that’s my fault.” He clearly didn’t let it eat at him as he finished the day with 75 yards, and when he’s the main target life is not going to be easy for him.

UNC Defense – Just a Herculean effort. This squad bowed up and bailed out the UNC offense time and time again. The only touchdown Duke scored on them was the drive on which they took the lead, and even that came on a very short field when the punting team couldn’t get a kick off and gave the Blue Devils the ball at the UNC 34. That sudden change is hard on a defense to stop, and they had managed to keep Duke to just two field goals up to that point. They also didn’t fall for the myriad of gadget plays that Manny Diaz seemed to want to try to consistently throw at them, almost as if he wanted to really show he could once again outcoach the great Bill Belichick. Diaz overthought it and the UNC defense made them pay. Yes, you’d love more tackles for losses, and the turnover didn’t happen until the last play of the game, but the defense is the reason Carolina won that game.

Losers

Turnovers – Duke went, effectively, 1-2 on the two fumbles lost for Carolina, and the first one was the only real reason Duke was in the game in the first place. While Carolina was deep in Duke territory, the offense had been effective and another sustained effort that turned into three or seven points might have completely deflated Duke for the rest of the evening. Instead, Shipp’s fumble reignited the Devils and completely killed Carolina’s momentum basically for the rest of the game until the final drive. The Tar Heels also couldn’t force a turnover until the very last drive. That’s not really a sustainable formula for the rest of the season, so Carolina needs to be better at protecting the ball, forcing turnovers, or both going forward.

UNC Punters – Aeron Burrell did not have a good day kicking, only averaging 41.7 yards on the day (and his longest was 43, so it’s not like there was one kick that killed his average). He ultimately was hurt at some point in the game, and so Adam McCann-Gibbs had to come in cold. The snap to him didn’t go well, and his indecision gave Duke the ball with outstanding field position. The Carolina defense just couldn’t respond — and honestly, who can blame them? — and put the offense in a difficult position.

UNC Offense (Post First Quarter) – Until the drive that started with 4:34 left in the fourth quarter, the offense that scored on their first three possession managed three punts, two fumbles, and a turnover on downs — which, technically, what that messed-up punt was called. The defense was playing their guts out consistently, keeping Duke at arm’s length, begging for the offense to get one more score so that they could get some space between them. The offense, arguably, was responsible for the same amount of Duke points as the UNC defense. A lot of it is at the quarterback position, as Billy Edwards, Jr. is just not a good quarterback. He’s fine. He’s better for UNC than Gio Lopez was for UNC — again, you wonder if Carolina hadn’t nuked that bridge what Lopez would have done in the Petrino offense — but there’s no reason why an open Shipp in the end zone should have to go through what he did to catch the ball. Also, Duke quickly realized just how important Shipp was to the team, and Edwards was so locked into him that when he couldn’t connect it just dried up. If Petrino and Carolina are going to stick with Edwards the rest of the season, they need to do more with his obvious limitations.

Honorable Mentions

Kenton Dobson III didn’t just have the big pickoff for the Tar Heels, he was also fourth on the team in tackles with two solo and seven total. Not bad numbers…Jelani Thurman had another solid day with 52 yards in catching but he had the other highlight of the day by laying one of the toughest stiff arms you’ll see on a defender and then ultimately getting hit out of bounds. He continues to shine as a portal addition….Demon June had the other touchdown for the Tar Heels with just a great red zone run. While he hasn’t put up the gaudy numbers, he’s put up great work deep on the field, and he’s settled into his role nicely.

This stretch of games rolls on as the Tar Heels finally return to Kenan Stadium for the first time since the Notre Dame loss to take on Syracuse. Carolina enter the second half of the year with a 4-2 record and only have to hit the road two more times this season. Can this squad keep the momentum rolling? We’ll see under the Kenan Stadium lights with the first night game of the season.

item.title: 10 Bears Takes: Caleb’s Comeback, Kyler’s Big Day, an Averted Collapse
item.description: After a disappointing Week 5, the Chicago Bears returned to the win column on Sunday afternoon in Atlanta. @AaronLemingNFL’s 10 Takes here.
item.content:encoded:
The seven-day break between their 31-7 beatdown loss in Green Bay and a second-straight game away from home in Atlanta was enough to make even the most level-headed of Bears fans lose it. In three hours, the Chicago Bears went from a great story that had started three quarterbacks in four weeks to a team that might not be very good. As usual, the narratives fly any time those two teams play, which can make it hard for anyone to turn the page. Luckily for head coach Ben Johnson and his team, they did just that. It helped that they got their starting quarterback back in the mix, but for the better part of four quarters, they looked like the same dominant team we’ve seen in four of their six games so far in 2026. Before quickly turning the page on this one for a Thursday night showdown with the New England Patriots, let’s take a deeper dive into Sunday and where they go next in Week 6’s edition of 10 Bears Takes. 

1. Caleb Williams’ return on Sunday was much-needed, even after a weird media session earlier in the week– why fans should feel optimistic about his play after a three-game absence. 

Williams ended last week’s Friday practice session as a limited participant, before doing plenty of work in Green Bay before the start of last weekend’s game. Speculation all along has been that he would be close to ready for Atlanta, and despite a Wednesday walk-through, it was clear they felt they had given Williams’ hamstring injury enough time and were ready to ramp him up. 

Then came Thursday, when his first media day in three weeks featured a long opening speech, some pointed statements, and a somewhat contentious set of answers. As always, people rarely take things at face value. Instead, everyone runs with their reactions, and it blows up into something bigger than it was. 

In the end, Williams came out on Sunday with some clear motivation to prove his critics wrong and did exactly that. His 83.3% completion rate was a career-high, and he eclipsed 300 passing yards for just the sixth time in his career. Taking out the anomaly that was the Vikings game in Week 2, so far we’ve seen a new version of Williams where he’s not wildly missing throws. Even more impressive, he’s continued to take what the defense is giving him. Even if those checkdowns aren’t turning into explosives, they are keeping opposing defenses honest, which is allowing for more shots downfield. 

To dive a little deeper into his six incompletions: four were throwaways, one was Colston Loveland overrunning a route in the end zone, and the last was a pass where his arm was hit mid-throw. Simply put, he didn’t come close to putting the ball into danger, and there were no egregious misses as we saw so often last season. 

Even though the offense scored 31 points, it’s easy to see how much was once again left out on the field. Between the penalties and missed opportunities in Atlanta territory, there’s plenty of meat left on the bone for this offense to continue to get better. That should give fans plenty of faith that they’ll keep improving as a unit, and ultimately, 40-point games are far from out of the question moving forward. 

No matter how you slice it, it was a great return for the Bears’ franchise quarterback. More importantly, the best is yet to come for this offense, assuming their core pieces stay healthy through the last 11 regular-season games. 

2. Speaking of returns, Kyler Gordon’s first game of 2026 was a stark reminder that when he’s healthy, he’s one of their best defenders.

Much has been made about his recent injury history and lack of ability. Frankly, it’s been justified considering these issues started after he signed his lucrative extension to make him the highest-paid nickel in the league. Despite his lack of availability going back to the start of last season, it’s impossible to debate that when he’s in the game, he’s one of, if not the best defensive players the team has. 

Gordon was activated off PUP earlier this week, which made Sunday his first game of the 2026 season. Despite only playing 16 defensive snaps, his three sacks and two forced fumbles were the most that have been tracked from a defensive back dating all the way back to 1982. Even if Gordon isn’t the most dynamic coverage guy in the league, his versatility is a huge value to any defense. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has always been known for getting the most out of his nickelbacks, and when Gordon has been on the field, the results have been no different. 

With the team’s secondary in flux due to injuries and their mix-and-match style, fans can expect Gordon’s snap count to rise each game until he’s settled into a full-time role. That likely means Tyrique Stevenson will go back to the bench, but considering how much both he and Jaylon Johnson have struggled down the field, I’m not sure that’s a bad thing. Fourth-round rookie Malik Muhammad should continue to see snaps on the boundary, and if that’s the end goal for him beyond this season, it makes sense to continue to play him there. 

We’ll see how things look once everyone is healthy (if that ever happens), but the offseason plan is starting to show. Once Coby Bryant comes back (hopefully this season), this could be a very different-looking group than the one we saw to open up Week 1. 

3. With a short week upcoming, it will be hard for this team not to look too far ahead to their 10-day mini-bye. 

It might only be six games into the regular season, but these last few weeks have taken a toll on this team’s health. It started with Braxton Jones a few weeks ago, and has since led to Dayo Odeyingbo going on Injured Reserve, while other players like T.J. Edwards, Stevenson, and even Kyle Monangai are on the “week-to-week” timeline. At first glance, the only notable injury the team sustained on Sunday was right guard Jonah Jackson leaving with a hip injury. I guess that we won’t get a better idea of what that injury looks like until closer to their game on Thursday, but combine that with Montez Sweat’s suspension, and this team is missing a lot of starting talent heading into their Thursday night showdown with a very good Patriots club. 

The Bears are in the midst of a tough three-game stretch that started with a road game in Atlanta, followed by a short turnaround with the Patriots, and then a Monday night showdown with the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks in Week 8. Before their win in Atlanta, going 2-1 felt like the “goal”. It would leave them at 5-3 overall, and ideally, it would give them tie-breakers over Carolina, Philadelphia, Atlanta, and Seattle, plus a 4-2 conference record heading into a stretch where they’ll see a 1-5 Buccaneers team, a Week 9 bye, followed by another favorable matchup against a 2-4 Saints team. 

That said, Week 9’s bye feels like a long time away, which means the early focus will be on getting through Thursday night and hoping for improved health during their 10-game break before heading to Seattle to face the Seahawks. No one would blame the Bears for looking ahead, and ultimately, if they can get some other important pieces back, it’s a win. 

The goal now should be to get as many wins as possible before heading into the bye week. For instance, going into their bye week at 6-3 would put them in a prime position to push for the division, or at least a playoff spot, heading into the second half of the season. The regular season is in full swing, and the Bears, like every other team in the league, must find a way to weather the storm and come out better on the other side. A small reprieve is just days away, but first, there’s a big game on a national stage waiting for them at Soldier Field on Thursday night. 

4. Following an ugly 31-7 loss at Lambeau Field, it would have been easy for the Bears to lay down and go into Thursday night at 3-3. Instead, they came out and dominated for 3 ½ quarters. 

We’ve seen this story play out before. Of course, that was before Ben Johnson and company, but the lengthy history of crumbling after a bad loss is well documented. So, in some ways, the reactions to last Sunday’s loss against the Packers were understandable. 

Going into Atlanta, it felt like a toss-up game that would come down to how successful the Bears’ offense could be. Ultimately, they dominated most of the game, and if not for taking their foot off the gas early in the fourth quarter, coupled with a Roschon Johnson fumble on the next drive, the score would have reflected how dominant Chicago was for most of the game. 

No matter the final score, make no mistake: Sunday was a statement game for the Bears, and it was good to see them rebound after such an embarrassing and emotional loss the week before. In reality, this has just been the DNA of Johnson-led teams since he took over in Chicago last season. After losses, the Bears are now 5-2 following a loss in the Ben Johnson era. To take it a step further, the Bears have yet to lose more than two in a row since last season. 

That should give fans confidence that no matter how bad things look and/or feel in the moment, there’s a good chance that they’ll find a way to rebound the next week, and usually in convincing fashion. It’s a good trait for any team to have, but something to keep in mind following any loss. 

5. Williams’ return and 31-point effort was a prime example of what this offense is capable of, even with all the meat left on the bone from penalties and prematurely ended drives.  

Although it seems clear that this offense isn’t going to set the records that Johnson had sought during the preseason, there’s still a lot of meat on the bone for a team that is averaging 25 points per game, while starting backup quarterbacks for half of those games. Their red zone woes have been well documented, but to their credit, they were 4-of-5 on Sunday. 

The biggest key is trading field goals for touchdowns and not getting bogged down in opponent territory. One remedy is cutting down on penalties, and after a few good weeks in that department, they took a big step back on Sunday with 12 accepted penalties that accounted for 133 yards. 

Missing Monangai has hurt their red zone offense, especially inside the 10. That said, the more Williams can get back into the swing of things, the more they can dial in their red zone and goal line offense. They have the weapons and versatile personnel to improve in that department and could also stand to get a bit better on third downs. 

All in all, these are situations most Bears fans have dreamed of being in before the arrival of Johnson and company. Their quarterback is playing at a high level, and in his three starts, the offense is averaging 31 points per game with Williams under center. Improvements will always be a focus for an improving contender, but the fact they are having this type of success with so much still to clean up is a very encouraging sign. The best is yet to come for this offense, and as long as Williams stays healthy, improvements should continue in the coming weeks. 

6. Injuries have continued to mount. Couple that with Montez Sweat’s two-game suspension, and the focus on improving the defense through the trade deadline needs to be a priority.

Those who didn’t watch the game will see Atlanta’s 23 points and assume the Bears struggled to stop the Falcons’ offense. The reality was quite different, especially in the first three quarters. In total, they had five sacks, six quarterback hits, and seven tackles for loss, in addition to keeping quarterback Michael Penix under 100 yards passing until the second-to-last drive of the game for Atlanta. 

All in all, Allen and his defense did an outstanding job keeping steady pressure on Penix, getting off the field on third down, and holding the Falcons to 0-for-3 on fourth-down attempts. With that in mind, they’ll face a completely different animal on Thursday against the Patriots. With Penix, the book is out: if you pressure him, he’s a bottom-10 quarterback throwing the ball. Keep the ball out of Bijan Robinson’s hands, and you have a good chance of stopping their offense. With the Patriots, Drake Maye is a top-tier quarterback, and they have plenty of weapons on all levels of their offense. 

Overall, Allen has done a nice job of getting the most out of this defense, but injuries have continued to mount for this group, especially on the defensive line. Odeyingbo going on IR was a tough blow, especially after how well he played as an interior pass rusher. Sweat’s two-game suspension hurts, if even from a name-value standpoint. Edwards had been playing well this year, and Stevenson’s continued hamstring injury hurts their depth at cornerback. 

Simply put, the Bears don’t have enough horses to win the race. The versatility at defensive back has been compromised due to injury and performance, but ultimately, they need another quality pass-rusher up front. Even when Odeyingbo returns from IR and Sweat from suspension, they don’t have enough difference-makers. The trade deadline won’t be a “be-all-and-end-all” fix to their problems, but it might be enough to keep them around league average. More importantly, it might help them stay more consistent week to week. 

We’ll see what shakes out in the coming weeks, and although I don’t expect a big move that sends any high-round picks away, players like Khalil Mack and maybe even Zach Sieler could make sense as lower-cost targets. At most, I wouldn’t expect either player to go for more than an early Day 3 pick. Don’t rule out another addition at cornerback, especially on the boundary. An old friend in Nahshon Wright could provide quality depth for a low price, especially if they aren’t happy with what they have right now.

7. These next two games won’t be easy, but at 4-2, the Bears have allowed themselves some breathing room if they can simply split them– More on how big of a win Sunday might turn out to be. 

Before Sunday, Pro Football Focus’ playoff odds had the Bears heading in two different directions depending on how the results panned out.

  • With a win, their playoff probability went to 64.3%.
  • With a loss, their chances would have dropped to 36.7%.

Now, it’s worth keeping in mind that the season is still very young. Injuries and general inconsistencies will help cloud, and eventually clarify, the playoff picture in both conferences over the next two-plus months. That said, the difference between 4-2 and 3-3 was big. Now, with two big games against both Super Bowl contestants from a year ago, a split in those games would yield a 5-3 record heading into a pair of winnable games with a bye week sandwiched in between. 

More than anything, seeing Williams back in action under center was a big confidence boost, not only for fans, but for this team to know what they are capable of. The next two games won’t be easy, and they have another tough stretch starting around Thanksgiving, but they’ve given themselves some breathing room, at least for the time being, with a chance to build on their early-season success. It might be easy to forget, but this same team went on a 9-1 run in the middle of last season’s schedule. If this team gets hot, watch out, because it won’t matter who they play; they’ll have more than a puncher’s chance in each one. 

8. Last Sunday’s loss to Green Bay and the overall reaction to it was a great lesson in not making one game more than it is- one game. 

I’ve said it before, and I’ll say it again: The Chicago Bears are a good football team. Sure, they have their flaws, but every team in the league does. No team opens the season and runs away and hides from everyone over the first four to six games of the season. It simply doesn’t happen.

Was last Sunday’s blowout loss disappointing on almost every level? Absolutely. The Bears talked a big game, had bragging rights for nine months, and despite not having their starting quarterback, they were still favorites on the road at Lambeau. By all accounts, it was an extremely deflating and borderline embarrassing loss to their most-hated rival. 

With that in mind, it was still just one game. In total, the Bears went 2-1 while starting backup quarterbacks. It just so happened that their one loss with a backup under center came against the Packers. Sure, their continued struggles in the division are a concern. Sure, you always want to beat the Packers, but I’m not sure losing by an interception in the end zone, or a 31-7 blowout, makes it any better or worse. The reality is, they got punched in the mouth, and now they have to live with that until they see Green Bay again on Christmas night. It is what it is. 

What surprised me was how many hot takes flew around about this team as a whole and their head coach. I’ll be the first to say that Week 5 might have been Johnson’s worst-coached game of his career, and that includes their Week 2 loss to Detroit last season. Context matters, and he has a great handle on this team now, compared with his second career game as a head coach. 

That said, the Bears are where they are largely because of their head coach. He’s instilled a new culture. A winning culture. He’s taken on the “bad guy” persona and has challenged his team to embrace not only the Packers rivalry, but daring to be great by blowing out opponents. Again, Johnson’s ego (to an extent) was on full display last weekend, but he’s proven time and time again that he can take something like that and learn from it. There was no reason for some of the columns to be written that everyone saw. There was no reason to question his viability as the team’s head coach or question his job status. That was all complete nonsense and emotional talk after one loss. 

Maybe this team never wins a Super Bowl under Johnson. Maybe they do. The one thing that is clear just a year and a half into Johnson’s tenure is that he’s the best head coach they’ve had in two decades and the sky is the limit for this group over the long haul. It’s easy to overreact to any one game, but in the end, it’s one game. That’s an important lesson to remember moving forward, because over the course of a 17-game season, losses will happen. How they respond has been the bigger tell, and so far, the team is 5-2 coming off a loss in the Johnson era. 

9. NFC North Lookaround: The Vikings and Lions enjoy early bye weeks, while the Packers hosted the Cowboys on a Sunday Night Football showdown.

This week, both the undefeated Vikings and three-win Lions enjoyed an early bye week. For a team like Minnesota, maybe it wasn’t as welcome as it was for a banged-up group like Detroit. 

The Vikings are riding high, and if history repeats itself, they are well on their way to finding themselves back in the playoffs after a disappointing 2025. According to Alec Lewis of The Athletic, the Vikings are expected to be active at the trade deadline, although it’s worth wondering what they will target. The defense has been elite, but the offense has been about as uneven as it gets. Starting in Week 8, the Vikings will face one of the league’s toughest schedules for the remainder of the season. While they’ve started hot, that will be challenged in the coming weeks. 

The Lions face much less certainty. Getting into the bye week above .500 felt like an accomplishment, considering their injuries and poor defensive performances. With a 4th-place finish, they’ll face a lighter schedule for the rest of the division, but their inconsistency has been concerning to a certain extent. The offense is still top-tier, but without a better defense, it’s worth wondering what their ceiling can be. They come out of the bye with back-to-back home games against division rivals, the Packers and Vikings. We’ll see how they fare in those games, but overall, their schedule is the most favorable thing working for them, outside of the high-scoring offense. 

Finally, we get to the Packers, who came into Sunday night riding high on a two-game winning streak, and an offense that is finally figuring things out. Despite expectations, it was not a high-scoring game as the Cowboys struggled to get their offense going all night. The Packers are now on a three-game winning streak and have looked markedly better than they did at the start of the season. Their defense is playing much better, and the offensive line has stabilized significantly. Starting next week, their schedule tightens up, but with the way they are playing, each game is winnable. 

Here are the standings after Week 6:

(5-0) Minnesota Vikings

(4-2) Green Bay Packers 

(4-2) Chicago Bears

(3-2) Detroit Lions 

10. Week 7 Look Ahead: Hosting the red-hot New England Patriots on Thursday Night Football.

After a slow start, the Patriots have figured things out. Not only have they won three games in a row, but they also have a +38-point differential in those three contests. Quarterback Drake Maye had a miserable start to the season, causing many to wonder if something was “broken”. The good news for Patriots fans is that his last three games have looked much closer to his MVP-caliber self than the first three games, when they went 1-2. Over his last three games, Maye has a 10:1 touchdown-to-interception ratio, while averaging 292.6 passing yards per game during that stretch.

So far, New England’s defense has more good than bad, and as usual, they are starting to get after the quarterback more as of late. As a whole, they have looked like a completely different team during this three-game winning streak, but it’s worth noting that they are just 1-2 on the road so far this year. 

For the Bears, this matchup challenges them in multiple areas. We’ll have to see what Jonah Jackson’s injury status is. Still, assuming he misses the game on a short week, the Patriots have a decided advantage on the interior with the likes of Milton Williams and Christian Barmore. New England has been borderline Top 5 against the run and has allowed less than 200 yards per game through the air. Offensively, they’ll have star receiver A.J. Brown back, and even if Romeo Doubs can’t go, they can stress opposing defenses in multiple different ways between the pass game and rushing attack. One potential saving grace for the Bears is the health of New England’s offensive line. They lost three starters on Sunday and are already without their starting center. With a short week ahead, the Patriots could play Thursday night with multiple reserves in the starting five.

All in all, this looks like a quality matchup on paper, but as we’ve learned, Thursday night games have produced unpredictable results. This is far from a “must-win” game for either team, but the difference between 5-2 and 4-3 is massive, especially with both groups chasing first place from behind the curve. Buckle in; we should have a good game on our hands.

item.title: The Morning After: Jalen Ramsey is the glue to the Steelers’ defense
item.description: Jalen Ramsey is the Steelers’ glue guy.
item.content:encoded:
Last week, Dave Dameshek asked me who was the one piece on defense the Steelers couldn’t afford to lose. I said that we may find out it was Joey Porter, as the Browns were able to have their way with the Steelers’ secondary and the cornerback room was wearing very thin.

It turns out the glue to the defense wasn’t Porter, though – it’s Jalen Ramsey.

The future Hall of Fame defensive back had one of the best games of his career on Sunday, totaling 10 tackles, four tackles for loss, and two sacks, including the game-sealing sack on 4th-and-8 in overtime to clinch a 26-19 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Lest we forget that Ramsey is doing all of this with a broken wrist that he suffered in Week 1. Yet despite that injury, he hasn’t missed a game, and his versatility has been exactly what the Steelers had hoped it would be when Patrick Graham said he would play the STAR role. Per Sumer Sports, Ramsey has eight run stops – that is tied for the league lead among all cornerbacks with Cooper DeJean of the Philadelphia Eagles. His two sacks are tied for second among corners, as Kyler Gordon made his return to the Chicago Bears’ lineup in Week 6 and had three in one game. His reliability in this role, combined with his tackling ability (only two missed tackles on the season) has made him irreplaceable. Players like Ramsey evolve as they get to the final holes of their career, and he has done just that. While he may no longer be the outside bump-and-run man-to-man lockdown cornerback he was in the late 2010s, his pure talent as a football player has seen him grow into being dominant as this Joker in the deck for the Steelers’ defense. Some guys lead with words, Ramsey leads by example – playing hurt, not making excuses, and showing that he is still more than capable of directly impacting the outcome of games.

It’s the morning after game day, and the Steelers are tied for the lead in the AFC North.

Jamel Dean’s record day

The Steelers signed Jamel Dean away from Tampa in the offseason with the hopes of forming a tremendous one-two punch at corner with he and Joey Porter. Obviously, Porter is now gone and Dean has become the top dog at the position, and he answered the bell against his former team with a tremendous performance.

Dean broke up six passes, which is a single-game record for the Steelers. Additionally, he allowed just three receptions on 11 targets, which is the second-lowest number of catches allowed when targeted 10 times this season. Who is first? His teammate, Asante Samuel Jr, who allowed two catches on 10 targets last week against the Indianapolis Colts.

And not to pat myself on the back, but when I made the Steelers’ mock schedule and predictions in the offseason, I said Jamel Dean would have a game-sealing interception.

Dean has been tremendous, and is a big reason why the Steelers currently rank top 10 in EPA against the pass and success rate.

Special teams struggles

The coach the Steelers miss the most was standing on the other sideline on Sunday. Danny Smith’s special teams unit was always a reliable one for the Steelers – the same cannot be said about this current group. Kaden Wetjen had a terrific 59-yard kickoff return negated by a Cole Holcomb penalty, which took the Steelers from starting at Tampa Bay’s 41 to starting at their own 20. There was another special team penalty on a punt, this one on Doneiko Slaughter. The Steelers were set to start at the Bucs’ 44 yard-line but instead had to start at their own 46. Throw in yet another Chris Boswell missed field goal, and you have a unit that has done a 180 over the course of just six games.

Quick hitters

  • Nick Herbig was awesome, recording his first two sacks of the season. Need to see more of that going forward.
  • We talked about it across our other post-game pieces, but what a performance from both DK Metcalf and Germie Bernard. Both stepped up in massive ways, combining for 22 receptions.
  • If the Steelers are going to be aggressive before the trade deadline, safety and linebacker are far bigger needs than receiver. Dare I say call the Chargers about Derwin James.
  • Congrats to Yahya Black for his first career sack and Daylen Everette for his first career interception. Big plays from young building blocks.

Let us know what you think in the comments. Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more!

item.title: Fantasy Football Week 6 Booms & Busts: Caleb Williams makes triumphant return, breathes life into Colston Loveland, Luther Burden III
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Scott Pianowski examines the biggest winners and losers from Week 6's Sunday action.
item.content:encoded:
The main window of Week 6 was not the prettiest selection of football. We dealt with injuries and underperformance, not to mention four pesky bye weeks. But at least we have Caleb Williams back in our fantasy lives. And that means the Chicago offense is back in business.

Williams was much better in real life than fantasy for Sunday's 31-23 win over Atlanta. He completed 30-of-36 passes for 305 yards, getting 8.5 YPA. He didn't run much (three yards) and he was limited to one touchdown pass, which means Williams came in under projection in any league. But he passed the eye test, and he got his playmakers back into the swing.

We can finally take Colston Loveland off the milk carton. Loveland returned a 6-65-1 line on seven targets, and the lone incompletion was on a wide-open opportunity at the left pylon. Loveland won on schemed plays and his touchdown came on a broken play, made possible by a Williams scramble and a confident throw into coverage. Welcome to the season, No. 84.

Luther Burden III also had a perfect day, catching all of his targets en route to an 8-95-0 log. Rome Odunze was limited to four targets, so his 3-39-0 was less than expected. But it was reassuring to see Ben Johnson clicking with the play sheet, dialing up play action and designed QB movement at the right times. So many of the Williams completions came to wide-open receivers; Johnson wins as much as anything.

The running backs scored the other touchdowns and thus returned their fantasy freight: D'Andre Swift (70 total yards) punched in two rushing scores and Roschon Johnson came through as a Hail Mary (15 touches, 85 total yards, TD). Bottom line, this offense can support a bunch of winning fantasy plays almost every week, so long as Williams stays healthy and Johnson keeps his mojo.

The Chicago defense can be a boost as well. Although the Falcons only managed 257 total yards and were never really in Sunday's game, they did collect 16 fourth-quarter points and made the final score respectable, pushing the game over the total. Kyle Pitts Sr. (the prequel to Loveland) had two of the scores on a 5-60-2 day. Drake London (4-62-0) was muted on 10 targets, and Bijan Robinson had the rare quiet day (53 total yards). But most of the time, the Falcons are an easy fantasy handicap.

Both teams get challenged next week — Chicago hosts the Patriots while the Falcons welcome the 49ers. Get your popcorn ready for both.

Speaking of the Patriots, they finally had their offensive skill sheet where they wanted it on Sunday. A.J. Brown (ankle) made his first start since Week 1, and TreVeyon Henderson (ankle) completed his miracle week of rehab by playing as well. Alas, both players turned into fantasy traps. Brown managed just 3-27-0 despite 10 targets, dropping multiple passes, a shockingly messy day. And Henderson was held to 40 yards on eight touches, in addition to a lost fumble.

Drake Maye's distribution this year reminds you of early Tom Brady — where the favorite receiver is the guy with the good matchup. DeMario Douglas (7-86-1), Hunter Henry (4-48-1) and Romeo Doubs (1-42-1) caught Maye's three touchdown passes; sadly, Doubs hurt his shoulder on the scoring play. Brown surely will keep target-hog status on this offense, but good luck deciphering patterns in the rest of this passing game moving forward.

As for Rhamondre Stevenson, he also underwhelmed despite a primo spot. He was limited to 36 yards on 14 carries, and Corey Kiner (11-57-0) helped drain the clock.

Forget what you thought about the Texans two months ago. It turns out the defense isn't so hot, and C.J. Stroud is probably better than you think. Stroud chucked for 312 yards and three scores as the Texans held off the Jaguars 34-31 in London — never an easy thing to do — and he thrived with a wide distribution, targeting 10 different teammates. It's interesting that despite the presence of Nico Collins and the trades for Kayshon Boutte and Marvin Harrison Jr., it's Jaylin Noel having a breakout year. He caught all of his targets en route to 4-107-1, his third straight game of fantasy relevance.

Stroud's efficiency was needed, because Woody Marks was underwhelming — 15 carries, 56 yards. The Texans get the Giants next week, then step into a Week 8 bye.

An extra overtime drive helped Jaylen Warren take a sad song and make it better. Sharing work with Rico Dowdle all day, Warren had a couple of second-level plays in OT and eventually made 78 total yards on his 16 touches. Dowdle had 10 touches for 49 yards and managed a better YPC. This rough 60-40 type of split can be assumed moving forward.

Germie Bernard (11-87-1) was the star of the passing game, winning on a bunch of quickly-defined routes and scoring the final touchdown. This was the rare day where Aaron Rodgers focused on his two main wideouts — Bernard and DK Metcalf (11-93-0) saw 27 of his 44 pass attempts. I don't know the Metcalf matrix — he's been inconsistent all year — but the Steelers should move the ball against New Orleans next week, so we'll keep an open mind. Bernard is quickly pushing into the Rookie of the Year mix.

Other Week 6 Booms

— Whatever you paid for Chuba Hubbard in August, it was worth it. Hubbard handled a lovely 28 rushes at Philly, rolling up 120 yards and a touchdown. The Panthers only used one other carry on a running back. Carolina's line is getting healthier, and Hubbard often gets more than what's blocked. Hubbard faces a strong challenge against Tampa Bay's front next week, then it's a bunch of fruitful draws — Packers, Broncos, Saints. He's looking like a possible league winner.

— Jameis Winston is the type of quarterback who can get benched on any start, and it happened again in Week 6 against the Saints. And miracle of miracles, J.J. McCarthy (243 yards, 11.6 YPA) actually moved the Giants in catch-up mode. Call it garbage time if you will, but we're just happy the ball kept arriving to Malik Nabers (12-165-0, 15 targets) and Isaiah Likely (6-99-1, 11 targets). The Ravens have to be kicking themselves for not finding a way to keep Likely; they tried, but didn't offer enough. It's hard to watch Mark Andrews play every week.

John Harbaugh has an interesting QB choice for next week against Houston. The Giants rest in Week 8.

Other Week 6 Busts

— The Ravens and Browns had a rock-fight type of game, with a meager 23 points and 472 total yards of offense. Tyler Huntley is obviously a backup quarterback, and Deshaun Watson should be one, too. At least Zay Flowers (66 yards, 11 targets) can look forward to the eventual return of Lamar Jackson. The Browns have assembled a lovely receiver room, but there's no one to deliver the ball.

— I wanted to keep an open mind with Tanner McKee, but 4.8 YPA against an ordinary Carolina defense doesn't feed the cat. At least McKee kept pumping the ball to the returning DeVonta Smith (7-75-1), who got home on 14 targets (say this for McKee, the touchdown pass was gorgeous). Dallas Goedert was also a reasonable play (6-61-0, eight targets), and at least Dameon Pierce (50 yards) applied some touchdown deodorant. Dallas is a great draw next week, but is McKee ready for the moment?

— Maybe the Rams aren't the Super Team they're made out to be. An 18-16 loss at home to Arizona is embarrassing, and there's nothing fluky about it — the Rams were outgunned and outplayed for three hours. A late rally bumped Puka Nacua up to 6-80-0, but Davante Adams was quiet (3-39-0) and Tyler Higbee didn't see a target (the Rams opted for a different tight end, as Colby Parkinson had five short catches and a late touchdown).

The Rams' backfield was closer to a 50-50 split, with Kyren Williams handling 13 touches (67 yards) while Blake Corum had 11 (60 yards), including a touchdown catch. The Rams have to ask themselves some difficult questions before next week's game against the Raiders.

— While the Giants were able to support their two primary pass catchers, the running back room was the ultimate false promise. Najee Harris was announced as the pre-game starter, but he did nothing — four carries, two yards. Cam Skattebo ran just six snaps and didn't touch the ball at all. Tyrone Tracy Jr. vultured a couple of touchdowns (one a nifty catch-and-run), part of eight touches and 45 yards. Devin Singletary also showed up, five touches and 33 yards.

It's a mess. The Giants clearly aren't in love with Skattebo, but no one else here has major upside. Tracy came out with the touchdowns, but he's always been something of a journeyman. I hope your running back desperation doesn't push you to the Meadowlands this month.

— The Green Bay backfield went nowhere, as expected, against Dallas. Pierre Strong and MarShawn Lloyd are not meant to be NFL starters, and the Green Bay offensive line is one of the worst in football.

I'd be careful with Josh Jacobs expectations moving forward. Obviously Jacobs has been a capable pro and just being tied to an offense that can move the ball — through the air, anyway — offers some fantasy value. But Jacobs is entering his eighth year, he might not be in game shape yet, and his YPC dropped to 4.0 last season. If I rostered Jacobs in any trading league, I'd make sure my opponents knew he was available. At least see what's out there.

First thing’s first: The Patriots won an important division game with real consequences. A loss would have moved the 3-3 Jets ahead of the Patriots in the AFC East because they won the head-to-head matchup. Instead, the win gave New England a 2-0 division record and solidified their 4-2 second-place standing ahead of New York. All good.

One troubling aspect from the game were the number of injuries. I’m still amazed how the offensive line depth rose to the fight in that moment. Despite different rotations and players moving in and out, the Jets’ sack-heavy defense didn’t get to Drake Maye once. I was hoping to see more players return, but without adding others to the wounded masses. Credit to Doug Marrone and the assistants for the way this unit responded.

The second concern was the turnovers. Drake Maye threw no interceptions, which was a good thing. But TreVeyon Henderson’s fumble in the third quarter followed by DeMario Douglas’ in the fourth kept the Jets in the game. Brutal. All in all, it never felt as if the Patriots would lose, but still a tad nerve-wracking when they couldn’t put the Jets away in the second half.
