item.description: The Bengals have opened up a spot on their 53-man roster as they return from their bye week.
item.content:encoded:
The Bengals have opened up a spot on their 53-man roster as they return from their bye week.

They announced that tight end Tanner Hudson has been placed on injured reserve. Hudson's agent announced last week that Hudson will miss the rest of the season after he tore his pectoral in Week 5.

Hudson had seven catches for 33 yards, including a touchdown in Cincinnati's Week 5 win over the Dolphins. Hudson is in his fourth season with the Bengals and his eighth season as an NFL player.

Mike Gesicki, Erick All, Drew Sample, and Jack Endries are the team’s remaining tight ends. They could add to that number whenever they decide to fill the opening Hudson leaves on the roster.

item.title: Deone Walker wrecked NFL’s highest-paid center in Bills win over Raiders
item.description: Walker was a monster against the Raiders
item.content:encoded:
Deone Walker is probably going to be the antagonist in Tyler Linderbaum’s nightmares for a while.

The Raiders made Linderbaum the NFL’s highest-paid center this offseason, inking him to a three-year, $81 million deal with $60M guaranteed at signing, and the Bills disruptive nose tackle demolished him for a large portion of Buffalo’s 33-30 win over Las Vegas in Week 6.

Now, Walker was only credited with one pressure on 30 pass-rush snaps, but he “won” his one-on-one reps with Linderbaum far more frequently than that, and he wreaked havoc against the Raiders run game, a ground attack that only averaged 3.3 yards per rush.

With this film session, let’s start there, and I’ll begin with the most emphatic display of Walker’s dominance in this game:

What’s the appropriate response to that rep? Linderbaum had become an elite-level center during his time in Baltimore, before he signed the monster free-agent deal in Las Vegas. He routinely won with a tremendous combination of balance, agility, and power.

Remember too, Linderbaum was an All-State wrestler in high school who famously pinned Tristan Wirfs back in a 2017 match between the future NFL offensive linemen.

Walker tossed the 6’2”, 305-pound Linderbaum aside like he was a practice-squad long-snapper on that rep then wrapped up Mike Washington for a short gain. All-Pro level highlight there.

At Iowa and early in his career with the Ravens, Linderbaum was a menace in the run game because of how rapidly he erupted out of his stance when either climbing the second level or getting to reach blocks across a gap. He regularly carried out those duties with ease. The movement element to his game is why Linderbaum was a first-round pick and a big reason why he signed such a lucrative deal in March.

Linderbaum’s speciality was irrelevant here against Walker:

And that is the exact type of block on which the smaller but more explosive Linderbaum should get the better of Walker. The clear win for Buffalo’s second-year defensive tackle wasn’t a fluke.

He had managed an even cleaner victory later in the game on a similar blocking concept that amounted to a tackle for loss:

I’m telling you — 6’6” and 345 should not be physically capable of shooting a gap like that on Linderbaum.No way, no how. But Walker did.

The majority of his pass-rushing opportunities featured double teams. Yet when Walker was given a chance to rush man-on-man, he either freed himself from the block or caved the pocket in front of Kirk Cousins.

This was the Raiders first offensive play of the game. Walker initially bull rushed Linderbaum, but take note of how he countered off it late it get a hand up near the throwing motion of Cousins:

That’s a reasonably high-caliber rep for a defensive tackle who probably wasn’t credited with a pressure on the play. He has regularly still impacted the pocket even when he’s been technically blocked.

And check this rep from Walker going full Swim Diesel on Linderbaum to force a hurried throw and incompletion from the Raiders veteran quarterback:

Through six games — before Monday Night Football — there are only three defensive tackles with more pressures than Walker’s 22. He’s been a stalwart against the run too.

At 22 years old, while playing 70.9% of Buffalo’s defensive snaps, Walker is playing like one of the best interior defensive linemen in football.

His performance against the league’s highest-paid center should remind everyone of that.

item.title: Fantasy Football Stock Report: C.J. Stroud finding form, Patrick Mahomes no longer sure-fire start after Week 6
item.description: Matt Okada goes over players whose stock is up and down coming out of Week 6 for fantasy football.
item.content:encoded:
As I write this on Sunday night, 13 of 14 Week 6 games are in the books (with Monday night remaining) and the season is continuing to round into shape. Sort of. There were promising improvements. Concerning trends. Performances that changed our early outlook on players and teams. As always, some of these shifting perspectives will have permanent ramifications in fantasy football.

With that in mind, I've compiled another full fantasy stock report. These are the most notable risers and fallers heading into Week 7. 

STOCK UP

C.J. Stroud, QB, Texans

I don't want to overreact here, but it appears C.J. Stroud might finally be rediscovering the trajectory he had at the end of his Rookie of the Year season back in 2023. It looked at the time like Stroud might be one of the best young quarterbacks and a future face of the league, then he seemed to lose confidence and precision over the next couple years. But watching him perform in London on Sunday, he looks back.

He completed 24 of 34 passes for 312 yards and three touchdowns (and one INT) and expertly maneuvered the Texans offense to a last-second win. He's now had 20+ fantasy points in three straight games, with multiple offensive touchdowns in all three and 307 passing yards per game. It certainly doesn't hurt that Nico Collins is healthy, Jaylin Noel is breaking out, Marvin Harrison Jr. looked better as a Texan and Tank Dell could return soon.

Stroud needs to maintain this pace for more than three weeks before we anoint him as a rest-of-season QB1, but the arrow is clearly pointing upward.

Germie Bernard, WR, Steelers

Germie Bernard was one of the top waiver-wire pickups of the week and he rewarded fantasy managers immediately to the tune of 11 catches on 12 targets for 87 yards and a touchdown. He ran 44 routes — two fewer than DK Metcalf — and the passing offense essentially ran through the two of them all day. With Roman Wilson out and Aaron Rodgers continuing to put up meaningful numbers, the second-round rookie out of Alabama is very quickly ascending into weekly FLEX consideration, if not higher.

Only 13 players have had 11+ receptions in a game across 32 teams and six weeks and Bernard is one of them ... among company like Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Puka Nacua, CeeDee Lamb, etc. That kind of production doesn't often fade into a supporting role and the Steelers offense needs impact players. It's particularly worth noting that Metcalf has not been as good or as involved as he was on Sunday in most of the weeks prior, so in his down weeks, Bernard might even be Pittsburgh's WR1. For fantasy, that makes him a must-roster player with must-start upside down the road.

Colston Loveland/Luther Burden III, TE/WR, Bears

Colston Loveland and Luther Burden III were two of the most highly touted and anticipated players in fantasy entering the season ... and both had been disappointments through the first five weeks. Burden was the WR26 entering Week 6, with just one game in double-digit fantasy points and zero games over 65 receiving yards. Meanwhile, Loveland had been an unmitigated disaster, with a season-high of 8.7 fantasy points and no touchdowns through five games. Both showed up in Week 6 with Caleb Williams back at the helm, finally offering some hope for the stardom we were promised. Burden caught all eight of his targets for 95 yards (all team highs), while Loveland caught six of seven targets for 65 yards and his first touchdown of 2026.

The easy interpretation would be that Williams' return made all the difference, but it's worth remembering that Loveland did absolutely nothing in Williams' first couple of games this season, so we're going to have to monitor this a little further. Rome Odunze was also quiet in Week 6, and it's not only possible, but probable, that there will be a bit of a rotation between these three throughout the year. Still, it was great to see that both players do, in fact, have the upside to dominate through the air, and managers can breathe at least a small sigh of relief amid previously growing "bust" concerns.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

Carnell Tate, WR, Titans

After a massive dud in Week 5 — one catch for six yards on five targets — we were forced to question whether Carnell Tate's breakout Week 4 was an aberration. Sunday's performance against the Colts (sort of) answered that question. The fourth overall pick snagged six of seven targets for 70 yards and his first NFL touchdown, topping 16 fantasy points for the second time in three weeks. He accounted for 54.5% of the team's catches and 68.6% of their receiving yards, and scored the team's only offensive touchdown.

On the one hand, it's concerning that this offense is still so anemic on the whole. It undoubtedly lowers Tate's overall ceiling and will likely make it difficult for the rookie to finish as a high-end WR2 very often. On the other hand, the fact that he's such a focal point for Cam Ward and Co. is certainly promising and should translate into fewer duds moving forward, as Tate continues to develop and grow into the league. Rookie wide receivers typically get much better for fantasy late in the fall and into winter, so these early signs are encouraging. It certainly doesn't hurt that Tate has, on paper, a very green schedule for wide receivers over the next couple of months. He's probably worth acquiring if you can get him on the cheap.

STOCK DOWN

Cam Skattebo, RB, Giants

Good gracious.

Cam Skattebo was one of my favorite plays heading into the weekend, considering the glorious matchup with the Saints ... and instead John Harbaugh decided to punish him for recent fumbling issues with zero touches on the entire day. It would have been more reasonable if the Giants' running backs who did see touches didn't total 34 yards on 14 carries, resulting in a 34-27 loss in which J.J. McCarthy was their leading rusher ... in one quarter.

The optimistic perspective here would be that this was a one-week lesson for Skattebo, and that the rest of the depth chart was so ineffective that he'll work his way right back into the RB1 role moving forward. But after literally zero touches (on just six snaps), the optimistic perspective seems more like wishful thinking. It's not like Skattebo had been incredibly efficient or productive outside the fumbles — with just 3.6 yards per carry on the year — so there's no guarantee he reassumes 15-touch-a-game volume. And it's clear the Giants' running game is a problem in general.

Skattebo's certainly not in the RB2 conversation right now, and it's not impossible he loses all fantasy relevance in the coming weeks. Check back in next week to see what Harbaugh does with this backfield.

Patrick Mahomes, QB, Chiefs

Patrick Mahomes is currently the quintessential case of "NFL success doesn't always equal fantasy success." The Chiefs are 5-0 and Mahomes had thrown multiple touchdown passes in each of his first four games, but after totaling more than 50 fantasy points in Weeks 1 and 2, he's averaged just 15.14 per game since Week 3 and scored a season-low 11.48 in Week 6. The primary issue, exhibited on Sunday, is that he doesn't need to carry this offense anymore — he has Kenneth Walker III for that job.

He threw one interception and zero touchdowns against the Chargers, but the Chiefs still won 22-6 as Walker racked up 128 yards and another two touchdowns on the ground. It doesn't mean Mahomes won't be a QB1 — he was the QB7 in points per game through his Week 5 bye — but outings like this showcase why he likely won't be the every-week star he has been in years past. You can still start him most weeks, particularly in contests that project to be high-scoring and close for Kansas City. But on that note, he has the Seahawks, Broncos and Jets on the horizon. If you have him, you might want to consider a streaming alternative for the near future, or trade him on name value.

If he's on another team, mark your calendar for Week 10 and think about trading for him then if possible.

Ashton Jeanty, RB, Raiders

Ashton Jeanty has become a regular in this section of the column and somehow he keeps trending down. And if you're glancing at his box score and wondering why, take a look at his carries and yards. The second-year running back managed just 22 yards on 10 carries this week after hitting just 27 on 10 carries last week. And this was a Buffalo defense that had been among the softest against running backs all season. Jeanty's averaged fewer than 4.0 yards per carry in every single game since Week 2 and fewer than 3.0 in four of his last five games. Meanwhile, Mike Washington Jr. played 33% of the snaps on Sunday but logged nine carries (to Jeanty's 10) and totaled a much more attractive 43 rushing yards (4.3 per carry).

Now, of course, Jeanty did score a goal-line rushing touchdown and caught four passes for 36 yards, so his 13.8 fantasy points ended up decent enough. The problem is that his value is dwindling down to just that: receiving work and touchdowns. And while the receiving work has been consistent, this was Jeanty's first rushing touchdown of the year. He's just the RB18 in points per game since Week 2 and has flashed very little upside over that span. You're essentially beholden to starting Jeanty every week, but he's likely to remain a low-end RB2 (at best) most of the weeks.

Jaylen Warren, RB, Steelers

Jaylen Warren had been a fantasy superstar in Rico Dowdle's absence, and his brilliant production in Pittsburgh's offense had given many (me included) hope that he'd remain the bell-cow back upon Dowdle's return.

Not so much.

He did still double Dowdle's carries (14 to seven) but that was his lowest carry mark since Week 2, as were his 50 rushing yards. Additionally, Dowdle matched Warren's four targets, which is particularly discouraging given how good Warren had been as a receiver the past few weeks. In three games with Dowdle, Warren has scored 7.8, 8.7 and now 8.8 fantasy points. Incredibly consistent ... and incredibly mid.

In the three games without Dowdle, Warren had scored 19.1, 14.1 and 33.8.

The drop-off is precipitous and disappointing. Worst of all, Dowdle was very good in his change-of-pace role, averaging 5.7 yards per carry, and it makes real-football sense for Pittsburgh to mix-and-match the two, as painful as it is for fantasy.

Warren is still a viable FLEX option moving forward, and will likely have a few more RB2 weeks down the stretch, but it's now much tougher to envision him as an RB2 on the season. 

Michael Wilson, WR, Cardinals

It's starting to look like the "Marvin Harrison Jr. was a great Arizona decoy" theory might hold some water. In two games without Harrison, Michael Wilson has had incredibly similar stat lines: four catches on seven targets for 30 yards and four catches on seven targets for 32 yards. After snagging 18 of 30 targets for 184 yards and a touchdown the two weeks prior, this has been a stark and concerning left turn.

Kendrick Bourne has picked up much of the slack and Trey McBride has continued his voluminous ways, so the era of double-digit targets for Wilson might have come to a rapid close. Now, with that being said, he did still see seven targets on Sunday, his sixth straight game hitting that mark, so Wilson's still undeniably involved. The problem is that with Jacoby Brissett at quarterback and the general inconsistency of the Cards' offense, seven targets isn't always enough for fantasy relevance in Arizona — see Wilson's four games with single-digit fantasy points for reference.

He's still valuable, but is dropping from WR2 range to FLEX range after consecutive disappointments.

item.content:encoded:
Week 6 of the NFL season is very nearly a wrap, with the Washington Commanders and San Francisco 49ers on "Monday Night Football" to close out the slate.

But before that, Monday morning brought some unexpected news, as the Colts announced they fired GM Chris Ballard, who's been in the role since 2017. Indianapolis fell to the Titans on Sunday.

Also on Monday morning, the Philadelphia Eagles and NFL agent Nicole Lynn released a joint statement on the status of Jalen Hurts, clarifying his diagnosis and treatment plan. He will reportedly be out for the season as he undergoes treatment with blood thinners after a diagnosis of a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and blood clots in his lungs, per ESPN’s Adam Schefter.

The Kansas City Chiefs, meanwhile, remain one of three undefeated teams after beating the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. LA is now the lone team in the league sitting at 0-6 as the seats of Jim Harbaugh and Mike McDaniel heat up.

The Miami Dolphins didn't have a chance to rack up a win while on a bye this week, but the Tennessee Titans sure did, walking away with the team's first win under head coach Robert Saleh on Sunday with a 26-20 victory over the Indianapolis Colts.

item.title: State of the Ravens’ roster entering Week 7
item.description: An updated look at the Ravens’ roster after an up-and-down first six weeks of the 2026 season.
item.content:encoded:
The Baltimore Ravens have been battered around in the first six weeks of the season. They’ve lost starters and depth players to both short-term and long-term injuries with several already on season-ending IR. With the Browns game now over, let’s check in on the current make up of the Ravens’ roster and practice squad.

Quarterback (3)

Active: Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley, Joe Fagnano

Injured reserve: Skylar Thompson

Lamar Jackson is expected back soon, potentially for next week’s game against the Cincinnati Bengals. He’s been phenomenal when healthy, and a 1-1 result in his two absences is not bad. Tyler Huntley did what a backup quarterback does: put together a solid game and then showed why he’s a backup and not a starter. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano remains on the roster as the third-string quarterback, though Jackson’s injury has elevated him to the No. 2 role for the last few weeks.

Running back (3)

Active: Derrick Henry, Justice Hill, Rasheen Ali

Injured reserve: Adam Randall

Practice squad: Jonathan Ward

Many expected the Ravens to carry four running backs rookie Adam Randall mysteriously landed on IR during 53-man roster cuts. There have been zero updates on his health since then, and no word on when his 21-day practice window before activation will start. The run game has slowed down in recent weeks with the offensive line shuffling and the injury to Lamar Jackson, but Derrick Henry still has seven touchdowns in six games. Hill has been explosive in his role as the third-down back, throwing blocks, catching balls, and mixing in the occasional 20-yard carry. He’s averaging 7.4 yards per carry this season, albeit on a limited sample size. Ali hasn’t seen snaps on offense and was putting together a solid contract year on special teams before multiple gaffes on Sunday in Cleveland.

Tight end (4)

Active: Mark Andrews, Matt Hibner, Josh Cuevas, Nick Vannett

IR: Durham Smythe (out for season)

Practice squad: Ty Pezza, Lucas Scott (FB)

The Ravens lost tight end Durham Smythe for the season to an Achilles injury in Week 4 against the Titans. In response, they signed veteran Nick Vannett off their practice squad to replace Smythe’s inline blocking. Matt Hibner also suffered a hand injury in Week 5 against the Falcons that has him out against the Browns and maybe longer, but head coach Jesse Minter said it won’t be an IR situation. Outside of that, the biggest problem in the room is Mark Andrew’s inability to transition from the YAC monster he once was to the possession tight end he is now. If he can transition into simply attacking the ball at the catch point and going down instead of trying to hit the button for the YAC option at the catch point, this room will be in better in great shape once Hibner and Josh Cuevas get involved as the explosive options. The latter had four catches for 44 yards and a touchdown in Cleveland.

Wide receiver (6)

Active: Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman, Tez Walker, Ja’Kobi Lane, LaJohntay Wester, Elijah Sarratt

Practice squad: Chris Moore, Gage Larvadain

This might be the best wide receiver room in franchise history. Zay Flowers has been undeniably a top-5 pass-catcher this year and leads the league in several metrics. If you’re looking at a graph on social media, he is probably in the upper-right (very good) corner of it. Rashod Bateman looks very comfortable in his role, shining when Flowers was absent in Week 2 and led the team in yards in Week 5’s win. Tez Walker is still fighting for more playing time, but his ability as a deep threat is apparent in how often he can be seen flying by defensive backs on film. And now, Ja’Kobi Lane has returned to add a contested-catch element everyone has been excited for since he started balling in OTAs. In his first game back he had four catches for 40 yards as part of a clear effor to get him involved. Sarratt is best known for a costly holding penalty for now, but he was always going to face an uphill battle for snaps. This group can be truly special once Jackson returns at quarterback and the pass game takes over as the driving force for the offense.

Offensive line (8)

Active: Ronnie Stanley, John Simpson, Vega Ioane, Andrew Vorhees, Roger Rosengarten, Carson Vinson, Emery Jones Jr., Cam Jurgens

Injured reserve: Danny Pinter (out for season), Jovaughn Gwyn, Ethan Pocic

Practice squad: Chuma Edoga, Kyle Hergel, Gerad Lictenhan, Andre James, A.J. Arcuri

This unit has been decimated. All three preseason starting center options are out long-term. Danny Pinter was declared out for the season in training camp; then both Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic were lost in Week 3 with IR placements shortly after. Their eventual return hasn’t been ruled out, but the Cam Jurgens trade seems to be signaling that the Ravens don’t expect those guys to contribute again this year. Rookie guard Vega Ioane has been admirably playing center in the meantime, with Andrew Vorhees and Emery Jones each starting one game at right guard. Ioane will slide back to his natural position once Jurgens clears concussion protocol and enters the starting lineup.

The Ravens activated Kyle Hergel and Chuma Edoga this week against the Browns as depth with both Vorhees and Jones questionable. Hergel is out of elevations and could be added to the 53-man roster as the backup center moving forward.

Defensive line (6)

Active: Nnamdi Madubuike, Travis Jones, Calais Campbell, John Jenkins, Broderick Washington, Aeneas Peebles

Practice squad: Rayshaun Benny, David Olajiga

This group has been led by the resurgence of Nnamdi Madubuike, who has picked up where he left off pre-injury as a dominant 3-tech, and Calais Campbell’s continued excellence in his 19th NFL season. Travis Jones hasn’t been bad, but he has not lived up to post-extension expectations. He missed a large portion of camp with a pec injury, so hopefully he’ll continue to round into form. John Jenkins and Broderick Washington have disappeared at times as the unit’s designated run-stoppers, and I personally continue to question their activation over Aeneas Peebles – especially Washington. Speaking of which, Peebles has been a healthy scratch since Madubuike’s return, despite the pass-rush win rates he stacked in the early weeks beforehand. Washington was sidelined in Week 6, but Peebles only got a handful of snaps. His penetration ability may only come into play in specific game scripts.

Outside linebacker (5)

Active: Trey Hendrickson, Mike Green, Tavius Robinson, Zion Young, Ethan Burke

Practice squad: Adisa Isaac, Kaimon Rucker

Trey Hendrickson’s return to the lineup could take this group to new heights. He was fantastic in his first couple of games while playing with a broken finger. He may lack elite counting stats, but his pressure and win rates match his film of a disruptive, productive rusher. In Hendrickson’s absence in Weeks 4 and 5, Mike Green stepped up massively with eight pressures and a pass rush win rate over 20%. However, he and his All-Pro teammate cannot seem to get going when they are both on the field. Tavius Robinson’s pass rush metrics haven’t been great, but he leads the team in sacks and continues to be a menace against the run. He consistently makees plays and could be pricing himself out of Baltimore this coming offseason. Zion Young has a solidified role on run downs, and his play strength consistently shows up on tape, even if his pass rush impact has been up and down. UDFA Ethan Burke nabbed his first sack against the Titans, but his role on defense will likely be minimized with Hendrickson’s return.

Inside linebacker (5)

Active: Roquan Smith, Trenton Simpson, Teddye Buchanan, Jay Higgins, Carl Jones

This group has been excellent, specifically Smith and Simpson. Smith is bouncing back from two down years following Mike Macdonald’s departure. Simpson has been a weapon, flying around the field with unmatched physicality. Outside of Kyle Hamilton, he has arguably been the best player on the Ravens’ defense in the first six weeks. The decision that will surround keeping Simpson and Smith’s cuttable contract next year will be fascinating to see this offseason. Teddye Buchanan will likely factor into that decision as his playing time continues to grow following the knee injury he suffered last year. He made plays last week in his highest snap-count game as the Ravens kept all three of those linebackers on the field more often to bottle up Bijan Robinson. Jay Higgins and Carl Jones mostly factor in as a special teams contributors; the latter has picked up extra snaps with Ja’Kobi Lane replacing Chris Moore on the active roster.

Cornerback (5)

Active: Marlon Humphrey, Nate Wiggins, Chidobe Awuzie, Chandler Rivers, Keyon Martin

Injured reserve: T.J. Tampa, Bilhal Kone

Practice squad: Amani Oruwariye, Lardarius Webb Jr.

This group has been up and down to start this year. They lost T.J. Tampa early in the season after expecting him to take on a significant rotational role. Humphrey and Wiggins have seen the majority of snaps outside, while Minter has occasionally rotated in Chidobe Awuzie. Both have made plays throughout this season, but multiple wide receivers have had big games against the Ravens. Keyon Martin started the season as the slot corner in dime packages, but rookie Chandler Rivers took over in Week 2. Rivers’ play has been a rollercoaster, especially in coverage, which led to Martin getting his job back in Week 6. There’s been little update on when Tampa or Bihlal Kone, who was placed on IR before the initial 53-man roster, could return. Either one of them would be welcomed depth and fit Minter’s scheme well.

Safety (5)

Active: Kyle Hamilton, Malaki Starks, Jaylinn Hawkins, Keondre Jackson, K’Von Wallace

Injured reserve: Jahquez Robinson

Outside of Kyle Hamilton, this room has been a massive disappointment for most of the season. Hamilton is, of course, playing at his usual All-Pro level. But Malaki Starks and Jaylinn Hawkins have had rough starts to the season. Both are playing with hesitation and simply looked uncomfortable in the first quarter of the season with tackling issues that hurt the whole defense. Starks has looked better across the last few weeks, especially during last week’s homecoming in Atlanta. The Georgia native played at 100 miles per hour and aggressively drove downhill against Bijan Robinson and the Falcons’ other skill players. In that game, Hawkins’ snap count took a big hit due to the Ravens playing three-linebacker looks, but he was back to a regular workload in Cleveland. The call for Hamilton to move back into coverage in tandem with Starks to help the secondary’s pass defense has been loud, but that would limit his impact around the line of scrimmage. Keondre Jackson continues to be the special teams demon he was last year and could be ready for a defensive role if injuries pop up. K’Von Wallace hasn’t seen defensive time and primarily offers depth on special teams.

Specialist (3)

Active: K Tyler Loop, P Ryan Eckley, LS Nick Moore

After tons of doubt about Loop’s position on this roster, the second-year kicker proved himself to start the regular season. He hit a massive game-winner against Dallas and converted his first five attempts over 50 yards, something he struggled as a rookie. He even set an M&T Bank Stadium record with a 64-yard field goal in Week 4. Loop did have his worst miss of this season against the Browns, mishitting a 49-yard attempt that proved to be massive in the loss, but on the flip side, the Ravens might be 2-4 without him right now. Ryan Eckley has been perfectly average as a rookie punter without any major mistakes, which is all you can ask for. (Remember Jordan Stout’s rookie year?) Nick Moore continues to be the engine of the unit and has even gotten involved on a few tackles.

The vision for this roster is finally aking shape after early-season struggles. If Lamar Jackson and Cam Jurgens are ready to play next week, the Ravens will field their best game day squad this season. While the loss against the Browns was brutal, there’s a clear path for this team to be very good if Jackson stays healthy and Jurgens raises the floor and ceiling of the offensive line. Younger contributors like T.J. Tampa, Adam Randall, and Bilhal Kone are all available to come off IR as well, which could cause some more roster shifting. Players on the fringes of the roster like Carl Jones and K’Von Wallace would likely be the first to if space is needed, but as always, injuries can make these moves clearer.

item.title: The Packers overcame disastrous first down results in win over Cowboys
item.description: A success rate south of 20% on first down isn’t a good recipe for offensive success.
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers had plenty of bright spots in their victory over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday Night Football, but the team’s first down offense was not among them. The Packers consistently shot themselves in the foot at the start of offensive series throughout their 23-13 victory, regularly losing yardage and requiring Jordan Love to go into hero mode on second- and third-and-long situations.

Fortunately, Love did just that, as he threw for 276 yards and a touchdown while adding a second score on the ground, all while being pressured on nearly 50 percent of his dropbacks. With the Cowboys’ defense consistently seeing big numbers on the yards to go category on the scoreboard, they were able to tee off on Love, hitting him several times and recording three sacks.

The fact that the Packers were able to score 23 points — a number that probably should have been more like 30, had their receivers caught the football in the end zone consistently — is truly remarkable given the disaster that the Packers put up on first down. Of the Packers’ 27 plays run on first down (not including one defensive penalty), the team failed to gain yardage on 13 of them, either via incomplete pass, no gain or loss of yardage on the ground, or an offensive penalty. That’s roughly half of the time that the team still has double-digit yards to gain after a first down play.

In those 27 snaps, the Packers managed to have a “success” (defined as picking up at least 40% of the required yards to gain) on just 5 of them. That’s a hilariously bad 18.5% success rate on first down, and consistently setting themselves up in long distance situations required Love and the Packers to have a 65% success rate on 3rd and 4th downs to make up for it.

Indeed, Love was 2/7 passing for just nine yards on first downs; on all other downs, he was 22/34 for 269 yards and a touchdown. (His rushing touchdown, a quarterback sneak, did come on first down).

The run game was no better than the passing game, either. MarShawn Lloyd, Pierre Strong, and Kaleb Johnson combined for 15 carries on first downs, gaining a net of just 25 yards. Because of the long distances, I counted only six true running plays on other downs. Furthermore, the run game had as many plays go for no gain or negative yardage on first downs as they had gains of four yards or more (four each).

And then the Packers also had three first-down penalties and a sack, only adding to the ugliness.

Here’s a look at the play-by-play results on first downs on Sunday night. As a warning, you may want to find an eyewash station after looking at this.

Again, it’s shocking that the Packers were able to put together a successful offense with such dramatic ineptitude on first down. Credit Jordan Love for being fearless and accurate in the pocket for this team being able to put together five scoring drives to reach the 20-point mark, and for putting still more balls in places where his receivers should have made plays and pushed the team closer to 30.

If the Packers can clean up their execution and start getting positive yardage on first downs with more regularity, this offense could very easily take a big step forward.

item.title: The Ravens found a loophole in the NFL rulebook, and ran the most creative trick play of the season
item.description: Here’s how this is actually allowed.
item.content:encoded:
The Ravens had a rotten offensive day on Sunday, largely because the team is a mess without Lamar Jackson — but one play caught everyone’s attention. In the first quarter we saw a 29-yard pass to tight end Josh Cuevas, who was lined up in the left guard spot, more or less tearing apart everything we know about offensive football.

The anecdotal response to this play is fairly universal: How is this legal? It just feels wrong to see a player move out of the left guard spot, catch a pass, and take it for a huge gain. However, this is legal in the rules — it just skirts around two elements of the rulebook to allow it to happen.

Firstly there’s “Position of Players at the Snap,” which states:

“Eligible receivers must be on both ends of the line, and all of the players on the line between them must be ineligible receivers.”

The Ravens still had receivers split wide as eligible, satisfying the first element of the rule — and on this play Cuevas was off the line of scrimmage, meaning that everyone between the two players on the line was ineligible. Furthermore, Cuevas’ position ensured he would not be an ineligible receiver as defined by the rules, because:

“Players who are not on either end of their line or at least one yard behind it when the ball is snapped”

Again, Cuevas was off the line — making him a legal, eligible receiver.

In terms of whether or not this will catch on, probably not. It was a really cute football play, but Baltimore OC Declan Doyle probably only gets one or two shots at this a season. Putting a tight end in the spot of a left guard off the line of scrimmage is just asking for a pass-rushing DT to absolutely blow up the tight end as a blocker, with the play relying entirely on the trickery of the defense not knowing who was eligible at the snap.

Moreover, teams will study this film and have their defense pay closer attention to both the positioning of players along the offensive line — as well as which players report as receivers pre-snap. Believe it or not, this play has been run before in the NFL. It’s not as if Declan Doyle invented the play, it’s just not used because, again, it turns out having five specialized blocking linemen in the NFL is kind of important, unless you want your quarterback flattened into a pancake.

Still fun to look at and realize how many elements of the NFL rulebook can still be bent.

item.title: Giants-Saints: 5 plays that led to the 34-27 loss
item.description: Five plays that were noteworthy in the Giants’ 34-27 Week 6 loss versus New Orleans.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants once again fell into a large deficit after establishing a 10-0 lead on Sunday. A special-teams fumble by Charlie Jones swung momentum fully to the New Orleans Saints, who scored 34 unanswered points en route to a 34-27 victory. J.J. McCarthy relieved Jameis Winston, swinging momentum back to the Giants. McCarthy led three scoring drives and threw for 243 yards in less than a quarter.

Unfortunately, it was a little too late for McCarthy and the Giants. Winston didn’t play well; he threw two interceptions and took two sacks. The Giants also — once again — had a nonexistent run game. McCarthy led the Giants in rushing yards on two rushes, and one of them was a loss of two yards.

The Giants’ inability to establish the run has led to a one-dimensional offense tied to an arm that’s historically known for throwing interceptions. McCarthy’s legs could help the Giants’ overall rushing attack. It’s still unclear when McCarthy will assume the starting quarterback spot, but it’ll likely happen soon; perhaps after the BYE week, if not in Week 7 against Houston. Here are five plays, or five sequences of plays, that were consequential and noteworthy from the Giants’ Week 6 loss.

Play(s) 1: Two-minute sequence, first half

Dennard Wilson kept dialing up the pressure, and Tyler Shough was feeling the heat. The Giants defense forced a 58-yard field goal attempt after the two plays below:

New York was up a touchdown, while receiving the ball with 1:18 left in the first-half. It was a comfortable place for the Giants to be; they dictated the game and controlled New Orleans’ offense, but the Giants’ special teams unit faltered. Charlie Jones fumbled the ensuing kickoff, which gave Shough the football at the Giants’ 28-yard line. New York’s defense still stiffened and forced a fourth-down on the two-yard line, but a BUNCH formation against man coverage led to Bryce Lance’s first touchdown in the NFL:

Chris Horton’s special teams unit has played well this year, but it allowed the Saints back into the game right before halftime. Jones MUST do a better job securing the football; the momentum was seized by New Orleans after the Giants dominated for much of the first half. 

Play(s) 2: J.J. McCarthy!

McCarthy relieved Winston after the veteran quarterback’s second interception. It was a 34-10 game, and the Saints scored all of their points consecutively, so the Giants turned the reins over to McCarthy with 11:25 left in the game. McCarthy threw an interception on his first drive that was intended for Malachi Fields, but it was a miscommunication between the two young players. However, McCarthy then led three scoring drives and gave the Giants a legitimate opportunity to win the game in the final seconds; it was very impressive. Here are some plays from the McCarthy led Giants:

Tyrone Tracy Jr. scored to start the comeback effort. It was his second touchdown of the game. McCarthy’s performance will cause a serious quarterback conversation for the Giants, as they head into Houston for Week 7.

Play 3: Can someone make a tackle?

I embrace the Giants recent pressure under Dennard Wilson. But if a team is going to dial up the pressure, they MUST make tackles on the backend, and New York failed to do so on this 31-yard touchdown catch and run by  Alvin Kamara:

item.title: C.J. Gardner-Johnson faces a potential suspension for spitting
item.description: The ejection of Bills safety C.J.
item.content:encoded:
The ejection of Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson for spitting on an opponent raises an interesting question, as it relates to the additional discipline to be imposed by the league office.

Last year, the NFL adopted a new approach to spitting. It now results in a one-game suspension, sort of.

It started when Eagles defensive tackle Jalen Carter spit on Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott before the first play from scrimmage in the regular-season opener. Because Carter's ejection covered the entire game, his punishment — a fine in the amount of a game check — simulated a suspension.

Later in the season, Bengals receiver Ja'Marr Chase spit on Steelers defensive back Jalen Ramsey. The officials didn't see it, so Chase wasn't ejected. Instead, he was suspended for the next game.

For Gardner-Johnson, the ejection caused him to miss half of the Week 6 game against the Raiders. Will he be suspended for another full game? Will the league fashion an NCAA-style targeting punishment that keeps him out for the first half of the Bills' next game?

Because Buffalo has a Week 7 bye, the clock isn't ticking as loudly as it ordinarily would be. Still, the league has a decision to make given the new precedent that was set in 2025, when the punishment for spitting morphed from a fine into a suspension. And Gardner-Johnson presents the first example of a player who missed roughly half of a game after being ejected.

item.title: Ups and downs from Saints vs. Giants
item.description: Plenty of standouts made an impact in the Saints win over the Giants.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints have finally ended their win streak, finding a win over the New York Giants. It didn’t start pretty, and it definitely didn’t end pretty, but New Orleans survived.

Up: KR Barion Brown

Rookie Barion Brown hasn’t been the difference maker on special teams that New Orleans expected when they drafted him to return kicks. But after some highlight plays over the past few weeks, Brown finally had his breakout game against the Giants.

Brown had a 41-yard return that helped open scoring for the Saints on the day, resulting in a field goal for Daniel Carlson. Brown would also have a 23-yard punt return in the game, setting the team up in good position.

Part of the Saints offensive explosion was their valuable field position, plenty of thanks to Brown. The former LSU wide receiver also recorded his first career reception in the win over New York.

Up: CB Martin Emerson Jr.

The biggest standout on Sunday is no other than cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. The veteran cornerback logged 7 tackles, all solo, a tackle for loss, 4 passes defended, and most importantly, 2 interceptions.

Emerson entered the game after Kool-Aid McKinstry left with what Kellen Moore described as a migraine. Emerson took advantage of the opportunity and became the team’s standout player and a game-changer.

With his big game, Emerson has now earned more playtime. It will be interesting to see how the Saints incorporate the veteran cornerback into their defense. Emerson was in a camp battle with Quincy Riley for the CB2 position.

Up: Saints’ running game

The Saints worked to establish the run, and found success doing so during Sunday’s win. New Orleans rushed for 175 yards on 38 carries, averaging 4.6 yards per carry. Kendre Miller led the team with 70 yards.

Three players for the Saints averaged 4.9 yards per carry or better, including quarterback Tyler Shough. Being able to run the ball is all the difference for the Saints offense. Instead of being stuck on third and long, New Orleans faced third and manageable more than not thanks to getting 4 yards on a run on first and second down.

The Saints offense has to prove that they can sustain success in the running game, but a strong showing against the Giants proves it’s possible.

Down: HC Kellen Moore

Weird, after the third quarter ended, I was expecting to put Moore as a positive after Sunday’s game. The Saints were looking pretty with a 34-10 lead after scoring 34 unanswered points. It looked like brilliant resilience by Moore and the Saints offense, who were called out by owner Gayle Benson earlier in the week.

Despite another slow start, with the Saints only finding points within the final two minutes of the first half, the Saints’ offensive explosion was brilliant. But of course, Moore has landed as a down for a reason. The Saints absolutely crumbled in the fourth quarter and were one play away from going into overtime despite having a 24-point lead with 10 minutes remaining.

This is all too familiar for the Saints, who found a similar way to lose earlier this season to the Las Vegas Raiders. Moore has proved his teams start slow and also can’t finish. It’s rare for a team that starts slow and also finishes slow to win a game, but Moore was lucky enough that his team pulled away with the win.

Down: K Daniel Carlson

Look, Daniel Carlson finished the day making up for his early mistake, but he hasn’t proven to be the consistent veteran kicker the Saints were hoping for when they hired him. Entering Sunday, Carlson has missed a kick in four straight games, including PATs, and added to that on Sunday with a miss from 55.

The veteran kicker quickly made up for it with a 58-yard field goal the very next drive, and another make from 51 yards in the third quarter. Despite his impressive comeback, Carlson needs to prove more to be consistent enough for the Saints’ offense to feel comfortable.

item.title: Colts fire Chris Ballard after mounting 10 seasons of mediocrity
item.description: Ballard took over as general manager in 2017 and will leave Indianapolis posting a 72-82-1 regular-season record and a 1-2 playoff record.
item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis Colts fired General Manager Chris Ballard, ending his 10-year tenure after a humiliating loss to the previously winless Tennessee Titans inside Lucas Oil Stadium.  It’s about time to light the match.

The final year for Ballard produced way more frustration than any success. Ballard took over as general manager in 2017 and will leave Indianapolis posting a 72-82-1 regular-season record and a 1-2 playoff record. Despite being given multiple opportunities to build a consistent contender, the Colts never won an AFC South title under his leadership and currently are in a five-year playoff drought.

That final defeat forced fans to file out early, while leaving a roar of boos to echo throughout Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday. Tennessee was 0-5 and had 11 consecutive divisional losses, which proves that loss was the final straw for an organization that has spent the last decade searching for answers. Indianapolis has lost four of its first six games to start this season and has been defeated in 12 of its last 15 contests dating to last season’s collapse.

For a Stampede Blue community that once believed it was possible to restore the franchise back to prominence, that patience had all but disappeared. Ballard’s tenure featured stretches of promise, but the organization never established the sustained success necessary to compete with the perennial AFC contenders. 

The biggest issue over his tenure is the endless quarterback carousel. Daniel Jones is struggling as the eighth different season opener starter over the last 10 seasons. Choosing to start the campaign with this awful linebacker unit, while drafting two linebackers that can’t seem to find playing time is another mark on personnel decisions. The constant lack of a pass rush is another stain that can’t just be wiped away.

Alec Pierce signed the largest deal for a free agent receiver in NFL history, but has played just 41% of the offensive snaps. The trade for cornerback Sauce Gardner has backfired as Indianapolis could’ve used those two first-round picks, especially since the 2027 pick may wind up inside the top 10.

This decision also marks a reversal for Principal Owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon, who elected to retain Ballard following last season’s falloff. Instead, the Colts have continued to struggle and the intensified questions about the direction of the organization have started to fall on her shoulders. Ballard, whose contract was set to expire after the season, acknowledged the shortcomings before his departure. He mentioned that he would not even offer himself another contract, recognizing that the results had not met the standard expected of the once-prominent franchise.

The Colts failed to capture a division title, gradually regressed and entered another season without a clear path back to the playoffs. The prolonged drought eroded the trust between the organization and its season-ticket supporters, many of whom waited years for a meaningful turnaround. Coincidentally enough, this week is when season-ticket holders are asked to renew their package deals. Good luck convincing fans to spend more for a comical product. 

Ballard’s departure leaves Indianapolis facing another significant transition as the franchise searches for leadership capable of restoring its competitive identity. The next general manager will inherit a team in need of a quarterback, receivers, a pass rush, and playable linebackers. Reminder that Indianapolis must find a way to build a roster that can compete consistently without a first round draft pick in 2027. 

After 10 seasons under Ballard, Colts brass decided that patience is no longer a viable strategy. The challenge shifts to finding the next GM who can change the culture from a decade of mediocrity into a contender.

item.title: Colts announce firing of general manager Chris Ballard after loss to Titans, DeForest Buckner criticism
item.description: Chris Ballard is out after nearly a decade as the Colts' general manager.
item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis Colts are moving on from general manager Chris Ballard. The team announced Monday that Ballard was relieved from his duties.

In a statement, team owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon said the team's standard "is to compete for championships." She added that she believes "a change in leadership is necessary to meet that standard."

Irsay-Gordon's full statement read:

"I am grateful to Chris for his years of service to the Colts and for everything he poured into this organization. He cared deeply about our team and our community, and we wish Chris and his family all the best.

"As I said at the start of the season, the sense of urgency has never been higher. Our standard is to compete for championships, and I believe a change in leadership is necessary to meet that standard.

"Making this change during the season was a deliberate decision. Waiting would only delay the important work that needs to begin now. We will conduct a thorough search for our next general manager and take the time necessary to identify the right leader for the future of this organization.

"I also want to be clear: this decision does not change our goals for this season. We have a lot of football in front of us, and I expect us to compete, improve, and win football games."

The decision comes with the team sitting at 2-4 after six weeks. It also comes after the Colts fell to the previously winless Tennessee Titans in Week 6. After the contest, Colts star DeForest Buckner expressed his frustration with the organization, saying he was "sick and tired of the same song and dance every year."

Ballard has been responsible for that "song and dance" since 2017. While he's experienced some moments of excellence — drafting Shaquille Leonard and Jonathan Taylor and signing Daniel Jones on the cheap in 2025 — he's also experienced some high-profile misses, such as drafting Anthony Richardson, hiring Jeff Saturday, trading a pair of first-round picks for Sauce Gardner and inking Jones to a two-year, $88 million extension ahead of the 2026 season.

Through six games, that extension looks regrettable. Jones has regressed after a promising 2025. This season, he's completed a career-low 59.6 percent of his passes, and has just four touchdowns against six interceptions, two of which came in the team's Week 6 loss.

The trade for Gardner has not only lacked results for Indianapolis on the field — he’s yet to record an interception for the Colts and hasn’t matched his All-Pro play in New York — it cost the Colts their first-round pick in April and (barring a trade) will mean they won’t have a first-round pick in the 2027 draft, either.

The team's next general manager will be tasked with figuring out whether Jones deserves to remain the Colts' starter next season. Even if that answer is yes, finding a long-term quarterback is almost certainly a priority for a team that has been scrambling for stability at the position ever since the surprising retirement of former No. 1 overall pick Andrew Luck in 2019.

item.title: Falcons sign QB Andy Dalton and release Cooper Rush
item.description: The Falcons add veteran competition for their backup quarterback job.
item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Falcons, fresh off a loss against the Chicago Bears, are signing veteran quarterback Andy Dalton. In a corresponding move, they’ve cut ties with fellow red-headed quarterback Cooper Rush.

To say this is a bit of a curious move would be an understatement, given that Dalton will open up as the third quarterback on the roster. Whether this is the Falcons covering themselves with Michael Penix Jr. getting banged up repeatedly and not wanting to chance Rush getting back into a game in case of a rash of injuries that takes down Penix and backup Tua Tagovailoa, or whether they view Dalton as a possible QB2 over Tua remains to be seen. Either way, Dalton’s a slam dunk upgrade on what the team had with Rush, at the very least.

It was recently reported that Dalton had turned down an offer to return to the Eagles, where he was Jalen Hurts’ backup until he threw an interception on his lone passing attempt in Week 3 against the Bears; the Eagles released him on October 9. With Hurts going on injured reserve and Tanner McKee, Cole Payton, and Joe Milton as the only quarterbacks in the mix, Philadelphia wanted him back, but he declined to return.

The path to playing time would seem to be much clearer in Philadelphia, which is part of what makes this interesting. One would think for Dalton to sign on he’d have to be given a legitimate chance to compete with Tua to back up Penix, and that’s my operating assumption until I hear otherwise.

Dalton has appeared in 180 games in his career with 139 starts, with his last more-or-less full-time role coming back in 2022 for the Saints. Originally a 2011 second round pick for the Bengals, Dalton finished his career second in passing yards and first in touchdowns in Cincinnati’s history. He has 254 career touchdown passes and 152 interceptions as his age 39 season rolls on and has typically been a solid backup at worst for the teams he’s played for, with a 66% completion percentage and 10 touchdowns against 7 interceptions in his last extended reserve stint with the Panthers from 2023 to 2025. It goes without saying that while his signing adds some intrigue to the backup competition here in Atlanta, my hope is that Penix is both healthy and effective enough that we never see him in 2026.

Give Dalton a warm welcome, and we’ll see if he can overtake Tua for backup duties in the weeks ahead.

item.title: Rapid Reaction: Colts announce firing of longtime GM Chris Ballard following brutal Week 6 loss
item.description: Colts longtime general manager Chris Ballard is out with the Colts.
item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis Colts (2-4), and specifically team owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon publicly announced on Monday that longtime general manager Chris Ballard has been relieved of his duties:

Ballard had compiled a 72-82-1 through a little over 10 seasons with the Colts franchise, having arrived in 2017. However, he had just two playoff appearances, 1 playoff win, and 0 division titles during his lengthy GM tenure.

While he initially got off to a hot start following his 2018 NFL Draft Class which included Quenton Nelson, Darius ‘Shaq’ Leonard, and Braden Smith among others, winning PFWA Executive of the Year for that elite draft class, the quality and returns of his subsequent draft classes largely diminished (aside from arguably 2020, which was a solid haul with both Jonathan Taylor and Michael Pittman Jr. in the 2nd round).

Never one to seriously spend in free agency, Ballard was notoriously frugal, preferring to re-sign his own players and maintain ample salary cap flexibility, despite glaring starting holes on the Colts roster year-after-year, which weren’t properly addressed. It was a major point of frustration among the Horseshoe Faithful and local talking heads because it just continued to happen on an annual basis.

That approach changed during the 2025 offseason, when the Colts signed both safety Cam Bynum and cornerback Charvarius Ward to lucrative, multi-year free agency deals, but by that time, it was too little, and too late. It’s a fair question of whether either one of those signings have dramatically paid off for Indianapolis either.

Having had two consecutive 8-9 seasons, and stumbling out of the gates to a 2-4 record, with no playoffs in Indianapolis since 2020 (the COVID-19) year, Sunday’s brutal home loss to one of the league’s worst teams was finally the straw that broke Ballard’s maligned tenure with the Colts.

The Tennessee Titans were winless at 0-5 and had an 11-game losing streak in the AFC South, while the Colts were at home and blew a 13-0 lead at halftime—with former franchise legends in the house to honor Adam Vinatieri’s induction into the franchise’s illustrious Ring of Honor.

Colts fans had been publicly frustrated with Ballard’s recent results, and coming off an offseason where Irsay-Gordon publicly proclaimed that, “The Stakes had never been higher” for the franchise, she made good on her word, as Ballard was finally shown the door and exits stage left.

At a certain point, winning results have to matter, and even though Ballard had a strong personal relationship with the Irsay daughters, the on-the-field product and collective talent of the Colts roster both have only continued to diminish. It was time for a change, and quite frankly, it was long overdue.

item.title: Miami Dolphins Trade Deadline Primer: The Top Candidates To Buy and Sell
item.description: From Austin Jackson to Brian Thomas Jr., a look at the players generating the most trade speculation around Miami.
item.content:encoded:
Miami Dolphins General Manager Jon-Eric Sullivan has already shown a willingness to sacrifice short-term talent for long-term assets. Last offseason, the Dolphins dealt Jaylen Waddle to the Denver Broncos in a move that helped build one of the league’s largest collections of draft capital entering the 2026 NFL Draft. As the Nov. 10 trade deadline approaches, the question becomes whether Sullivan has another move or two up his sleeve. National analysts have identified several Dolphins as potential trade candidates, with three names appearing more often than the rest: Austin Jackson, Joshua Uche and Zach Sieler.

The Dolphins as Sellers

T Austin Jackson 

  • Alain Poupart, Sports Illustrated: “Jackson is scheduled to become a free agent after the season and he’s got a low base salary that would make him attractive financially to other teams.”
  • Carter Bahns, CBS Sports: “Tackles are always in demand. He would be an affordable half-season rental.”
  • Anthony DiMoro, Heavy: “With offensive lines such as the Philadelphia Eagles decimated either by departures or injuries, Jackson immediately steps in as a starting right tackle for the majority of offensive line-starved teams in the NFL.”
  • Kyle Crabbs, Yahoo Sports: “Given his durability concerns and lack of a low end contract, Jackson has the makings of a perfect insurance rental at offensive tackle for a contending team.” Potential buyer: Jaguars, which is currently without standout tackle Anton Harrison.

It’s easy to see why Jackson has emerged as the consensus favorite to be moved. Starting-caliber offensive tackles rarely become available, and Miami has already spent much of the season evaluating younger offensive linemen. If Sullivan is looking for the cleanest path to adding draft capital, Jackson may be it.

EDGE Joshua Uche

  • Alex Kay, Bleacher Report: “Parting with a late-round pick to bolster the defensive front with a player who recorded 11.5 sacks as recently as the 2022 season is worth the risk.” Potential buyer: Ravens 
  • Dan Graziano, ESPN: “He’s a seven-year veteran who’s playing well for a team in the first year of a significant rebuild. If the Dolphins get the opportunity to turn this signing into a useful draft pick, it’s not at all hard to imagine them jumping on it.”

Uche presents the opposite dilemma. Unlike Jackson, there appears to be a real argument for keeping him: He has played well, fits the age profile of a player who could still contribute when Miami is ready to compete again and likely wouldn’t command a massive contract extension. The question becomes whether the Dolphins value a future draft pick more than continuity in the pass rush.

DT Zach Sieler

  • Poupart: “Sieler is coming off his best performance of the season and he remains a solid, at times very good, interior defensive lineman, but he will be 32 at the start of the 2026 season. That could be a problem for Miami, though not for a contender looking for D-line help.” 
  • Antwan Staley, Athlon Sports: “With no guaranteed money remaining on his contract after the 2026 season, the Dolphins could release Sieler next offseason. Ideally, they’d like at least an early Day 3 pick, possibly from a contending team that needs interior defensive help.”
  • Jason La Canfora, Casino.org: “While Sieler is now in his 30s, he continues to draw double teams at the line of scrimmage despite limited help around him. As Miami seeks to accumulate draft capital, Sieler becomes a prime trading chip.”

Sieler is arguably Miami’s best trade chip, but he’s also the player who would be hardest to replace. While most rebuilding teams listen when contenders come calling about veterans in their 30s, moving one of the locker room’s most respected veterans would send a signal that Miami is prioritizing future assets over short-term competitiveness.

While a handful of Dolphins have surfaced in trade speculation, those three names consistently appeared across multiple national outlets. It’s worth noting that trading Sieler would result in a $10 million dead cap for 2026 and a $24+ million dead cap for 2027. A Jackson trade would result in a $4.5 million dead cap for 2026 and $14 million in 2027. Trading Uche would result in a dead cap for 2026 of just $600,000. (These stats courtesy of Spotrac.) 

Other Names To Watch

None of these players surfaced as frequently as Jackson, Uche, or Sieler, but each has factors that could make him expendable if Miami receives the right offer.

LB Willie Gay Jr. 

  • Justin Carter, Fansided: “With Rodriguez and Brooks both playing 90 percent or more of snaps, Gay’s 50 percent snap share can be replaced by getting Jackson Woodard or Liam Anderson on the field more.”

WR Jalen Tolbert

  • James Brizuela, Yahoo Sports: “Tolbert may not be utilized in the correct way with the Dolphins, but he could be a strong rotational option for another team that needs a boost to their wide receiver department.”

S Zayne Anderson

  • Carter: “Anderson ranks 30th among safeties in PFF grade. He’s only allowed two receptions all season and ranks first among safeties in yards allowed per reception.”

The Dolphins as Buyers?

While most trade deadline discussion has focused on the Dolphins as sellers, Miami could just as easily explore opportunities to acquire young talent. The roster remains one of the league’s youngest, and rebuilding teams sometimes use the deadline to take chances on players whose value has dipped elsewhere. The Dolphins have only $6 million and change in cap room for 2026, which limits who they might be able to bring in. Just the same, here are a few names to keep an eye out for:

Jaguars WR Brian Thomas Jr.

One of the most discussed trade targets this season, Thomas is two years removed from a 1,200-yard, 10-touchdown rookie season that earned him a Pro Bowl nod. He’s young (24) and still on his rookie contract, which as a former first-round pick includes a fifth-year option. His affordability and potential could cost a Day 2 pick in the 2027 draft, making him a more expensive target than others on this list.

Vikings WR Jauan Jennings

Back in the offseason, the Miami Herald’s Barry Jackson reported the team was interested in then-free agent Jennings, who ended up signing an $8 million one-year deal with the Vikings. The 29-year-old has been a dud in Minnesota this season (2 receptions for 9 yards), but the previous two years Jennings caught 15 touchdowns and 1,600 yards for the 49ers. Adding him would cost the Dolphins maybe $2 million the rest of the season but give the team a reliable possession receiver already familiar with Bobby Slowik’s offense.

Titans DL Solomon Thomas

The Dolphins are already in need of defensive line help, a need that will become even more pressing if they trade Uche. Maybe they can rehab another veteran lineman in Solomon Thomas, who has 18.5 sacks and 145 tackles over a 10-year career. Now, it’s possible he’s washed up, but at low salary ($1-2 million) and acquisition costs, he might be worth a look.

Browns WR Jerry Jeudy

Two years off a 1,200-yard Pro Bowl season, Jeudy is languishing with the Browns (12 receptions for 150 yards) and ranks fifth on the team in receptions. The 27-year-old could probably be had for a Day 3 pick, and the Dolphins would only owe him about $1 million for the rest of the season. Jeudy has a non-guaranteed $22.9 million salary for 2027 that would need to be restructured.

Whether the Dolphins ultimately buy, sell or do some combination of both, the deadline should offer another glimpse into Sullivan’s long-term vision. Last offseason he was willing to move a popular player like Jaylen Waddle in exchange for future assets. If a contender comes calling for Austin Jackson, Joshua Uche, Zach Sieler or some other veteran, we’ll see whether that philosophy still applies.

item.title: Chiefs Week 6 snap count analysis: Andrew Armstrong steps up
item.description: Here are the important notes from Kansas City’s snap-count breakdown in the Week 6 win.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis!

Let’s take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs’ snap counts in the 22-6 win over the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 6. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus’ premium stats.

Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Jaylon Moore, QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Andrew Armstrong, WR Xavier Worthy, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Travis Kelce and TE Noah Gray

Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, DT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Drue Tranquill, CB Christian Roland-Wallace, CB Mansoor Delane, CB Nohl Williams, S Alohi Gilman and S Chamarri Conner

Did not play: QB Justin Fields

Inactive: TE Jared Wiley, QB Garrett Nussmeier (Emergency third QB), DB Jadon Canady, DE Jack Pyburn, OT Diego Pounds, LT Josh Simmons (Back), WR Rashee Rice (Hamstring)

The big takeaway: Andrew Armstrong steps up in first career start

With wide receiver Rashee Rice (hamstring) ruled out on the final injury report, the Chiefs elevated second-year wideout Andrew Armstrong from the practice squad. He lined up on the opening snap, marking his first career start.

It was the first of 42 snaps Armstrong played on offense, starting alongside Xavier Worthy (51) and Jalen Royals (45); he caught a 13-yard pass on one of the two passes thrown his way.

Armstrong spent 12 snaps in the slot and 14 snaps on the perimeter of the offense, signaling the use of Armstrong’s blocking near the line of scrimmage on run plays. He lined up for 15 run plays, nearly as much as Worthy (18) and Royals (17).

I don’t need a PFF “run-blocking” grade to know Armstrong was an impactful blocker. With an offense built around running back Kenneth Walker gashing defenses, the question becomes whether Armstrong deserves a spot on the active roster, maybe in favor of the return specialist Nikko Remigio.

The Offensive takeaway: Joshua Ezeudu plays the whole second half

After right tackle Jaylon Moore entered concussion protocol late in the first half, backup Joshua Ezeudu took over on the right edge and stayed there for the rest of the afternoon. He played 30 snaps, 17 of them on pass plays.

PFF faulted Ezeudu with one pressure and a hurry, so he kept Mahomes clean in his first time in the lineup for the Chiefs’ offense. After the preseason, he was traded to Kansas City from the New York Giants after spending most of his career at left guard or tackle with Big Blue. It will be interesting to see whether the lineup shifts moving forward, even if left tackle Josh Simmons (back) isn’t ready for Week 7.

Also noteworthy is third tight end Jake Briningstool, who played the most snaps (10) he has since Week 1 and made an impactful block to spring running back Kenneth Walker for the 33-yard touchdown run in the first quarter.

The Defensive takeaway: Ashton Gillotte ascends in the rotation

Second-year defensive end Ashton Gillotte played the fourth-most snaps among the team’s defensive linemen on Sunday, on the field for 52% of the defense’s snaps.

In that time, he registered three pressures: a hurry, a quarterback hit and a sack that broke the seal on the Chiefs’ four-sack game. He earned two “Stops,” tackles that count as failures for the offense.

It was Gillotte’s biggest timeshare in the Chiefs’ starting lineup this season, and his most impactful performance. He, along with rookie edge rusher R Mason Thomas (five pressures), was constantly in the backfield on Sunday afternoon and is a positive indicator for the pass rush moving forward.

item.title: Week 6 AFC West roundup, Las Vegas’ divisional title hopes slipping away
item.description: Checking in on the rest of the division as the Raiders slide down the standings
item.content:encoded:
Just a few weeks ago, the Las Vegas Raiders battled the Kansas City Chiefs for first place in the AFC West. However, with the Raiders falling to 3-3 after the Week 6 loss to the Buffalo Bills, Las Vegas’ divisional title hopes are slipping away. With that in mind, let’s see how the weekend went for the Denver Broncos, Los Angeles Chargers and Chiefs.

Broncos vs. Seahawks

Score: 17-14 (OT) Broncos win

Key Stats:

  • QB Bo Nix: 17/27 (63.0%), 107 yards, 0 TDs, 0 INTs
  • RB RJ Harvey: 6 carries, 25 yards, 1 TD, 3 catches, 31 receiving yards
  • WR Jaylen Waddle: 4 catches, 24 yards
  • CB Ja’Quan McMillian: 5 tackles, 1 sack, 2 PDs, 1 INT
  • DT Zach Allen: 5 tackles, 0.5 sack, 2 PDs

Nix is the big storyline from this game, especially with Ryan Fitzpatrick’s strong comments, saying the Broncos’ signal caller is being “disrespectful to the quarterback position.” That’s primarily due to Nix refusing to push the ball down the field, as completing 17 passes and barely cracking triple-digit yards is an eye-popping stat line, and not in a good way. Even with Sean Payton calling the plays for the second week in a row, the Broncos’ offense hasn’t shown much. Denver put up 14 points in the second quarter and didn’t score again until a Sam Darnold interception in overtime set up the Broncos with a short field for the game-winning field goal.

Next week: @ Cardinals

Chargers vs. Chiefs

Score: 22-6 Chiefs win

KC Key Stats:

  • QB Patrick Mahomes: 23/30 (76.7%), 272 yards, 0 TDs, 1 INT, 5 rushes, 16 rushing yards
  • RB Kenneth Walker III: 19 carries, 128 yards, 2 TDs, 2 catches, 11 receiving yars
  • WR Xavier Worthy: 7 catches, 73 yards
  • EDGE George Karlaftis: 6 tackles, 1 sack, 2 TFLs, 2 PDs, 3 QB hits
  • LB Nick Bolton: 11 tackles

LAC Key Stats:

  • QB Justin Herbert: 22/37 (59.5%), 204 yards, 0 TDs, 1 INT, 5 rushes, 26 rushing yards
  • RB Kimani Vidal: 7 rushes, 21 yards
  • WR Quentin Johnston: 1 catch, 57 yards
  • CB Cam Hart: 4 tackles, 1 INT
  • CB Tarheeb Still: 8 tackles, 1 TFL

This game went how everyone expected. The Chiefs had two weeks to prepare for one of the worst teams in the NFL, and the results showed on the field. The Chargers’ offense continues to be abysmal, as the team amassed just 259 yards and Herbert was the leading rusher. Meanwhile, Kansas City scored on its opening possession and never looked back, as Walker continues to run through the entire league. The reigning Super Bowl MVP has rushed for triple digits in four out of five games, and the defense has kept opponents to 10 or fewer points three times.

KC Next Week: @ Seahawks (SNF)

LAC Next Week: Bye

Standings

  1. Kansas City 5-0 (+57 point differential)
  2. Denver 4-2 (-11)
  3. Las Vegas 3-3 (0)
  4. Los Angeles 0-6 (-61)

In Other Raiders’ Links:

  • What we learned against Bills: “The Raiders’ ground game had some success in the second half, but it also struggled at times,” S&BP’s Bill Williamson wrote. “Starter Ashton Jeanty had just 22 yards on 10 carries. Rookie Mike Washington got involved after not being a big part of the plan last week, and he responded with two 10-plus-yard runs. He finished with 43 yards on nine carries. Yet, the Raiders are still looking for consistency in this area.”
  • Raiders road dogs in Week 7: According to our friends at FanDuel Sportsbook, Las Vegas is opening as a 5.5-point underdog against the Los Angeles Rams next week.
  • Tyler Linderbaum recaps performance: “I didn’t feel good about it,” the center said, via Raider Nation Radio’s X/Twitter account. “I let 96 (Deone Walker) dictate the game on me…I just gotta play better for the team.”
  • No moral victories: “Very disappointed that we didn’t get it done today,” Klint Kubiak said, via Levi Edwards of the team’s website. “Credit to Buffalo, they played a great game. As a team, we did not close the game and there’s plenty of improvement. We’re not satisfied with any moral victories.”
